story.title: Juno and the Buzzy Door
story.subtitle: A golden dinosaur, a hive full of friends, and one tiny drop of honey.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Buzzy Door
chapters.text:
Juno sat on her bedroom floor. Her toy dinosaur Rex stomped across the rug.

STOMP. STOMP. STOMP.

Then Rex began to glow. Gold light. Soft buzzing. BZZZZ.

A little door opened in the rug. Inside, something golden and sparkly.

It was a bee! Stuck in a drop of old golden stone called **amber**.

"Whoa," said Juno. "Was that bee a dinosaur friend?"

Rex's eyes blinked. "Yes!" he buzzed. "Bees buzzed around **way back**, when dinosaurs stomped too."

Juno grinned. "Then let's go meet them!"

Rex flapped tiny wings. BZZZZ. The door grew bigger. Juno climbed through, into golden light.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Big Buzzing House
chapters.text:
WHOOSH! Juno landed in a huge, humming house.

It smelled sweet, like flowers and honey.

"This is a bee home," said Rex. "It can hold **thousands** of bees!"

Juno counted on her fingers. "That's a LOT."

"There is one queen bee," said Rex. "She's the mom of them all."

"And lots and lots of worker bees," he added. "They are all girls."

"And some boy bees called **drones**," he said. "They don't make honey."

Juno giggled. "Boy bees get to relax?"

"A little bit," buzzed Rex.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Busy Queen
chapters.text:
Buzzing bees zoomed past Juno's nose.

In the middle sat a big bee wearing a shiny stripe.

"That's the queen," said Rex.

Juno watched her lay tiny white eggs, one after another.

"She lays up to **two thousand** eggs," said Rex. "Every single day, in busy spring!"

Juno's eyes went wide. "That's more eggs than I can count!"

"Way more," laughed Rex.

Juno patted the air gently, like clapping for the queen. "Good job, Queen Bee!"

The queen kept laying eggs, busy as ever.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Every Bee Has a Job
chapters.text:
Worker bees buzzed every which way.

One swept a tiny room clean. Another stood guard at the door.

"They take turns doing every job," said Rex.

Juno pointed at a bee zooming outside. "What's she doing?"

"She's flying out to find flowers," said Rex.

Juno grinned. "I want a job too!"

"You already have one," said Rex. "Chief Flower Spotter."

Juno spotted a yellow flower through the door. "THERE'S ONE!"

The worker bee buzzed off toward it. Juno waved. "Good luck!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Five Eyes and Zoom Wings
chapters.text:
A bee landed close to Juno's nose.

"Look at her eyes," said Rex.

Juno counted. "One, two... she has lots!"

"Five eyes," said Rex. "Two big ones for seeing, three tiny ones on top for sensing light."

Juno blinked her own two eyes. "I only have two!"

The bee's wings flapped so fast they blurred.

"Her wings flap **two hundred times every second**," said Rex. "That makes the buzzing sound."

Juno flapped her arms like wings. "Like THIS?"

"Almost," laughed Rex. "But bees are much, much faster."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Six-Sided Rooms
chapters.text:
Juno looked at the walls of the hive.

Tiny rooms, each with six sides, filled every space.

"Those are called honeycomb cells," said Rex. "Shaped like little six-sided rooms."

"Why six sides?" asked Juno.

"Six sides hold the most honey," said Rex, "using the least wax to build them."

Juno traced one shape with her finger. "Like a tiny honey house!"

"Exactly," said Rex. "Can you guess what shape this is?"

Juno thought hard. "A hexagon!"

"Smart bee-spotter," cheered Rex.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: One Tiny Drop
chapters.text:
A worker bee landed on a flower outside the door.

She drank the sweet juice inside, called **nectar**.

"One bee only makes a tiny, tiny drop of honey," said Rex. "In her whole life!"

Juno frowned. "That's not much."

"But bees work together," said Rex. "Lots of bees visit **millions** of flowers, to make just one jar of honey."

Juno looked at all the buzzing bees around her. "Teamwork!"

"Big teamwork," agreed Rex.

Juno clapped her hands. "GO TEAM BEE!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Oldest Honey
chapters.text:
Rex showed Juno a picture of an old clay pot.

"People found honey in pots from a long, long time ago," said Rex. "It was still good to eat!"

Juno gasped. "Still yummy? After THAT long?"

"Honey almost never goes bad," said Rex. "It stays sweet and safe."

Juno smiled. "Honey is magic."

The golden light began to fade. BZZZZ, softer now.

Juno blinked, and she was back on her rug. Rex sat still again, a toy dinosaur once more.

But on the carpet beside him sat one tiny golden drop, shaped like a honeycomb cell.

Juno yawned and hugged Rex close.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Juno. Buzz well, dream well.

A bee has **five eyes**: two big ones for seeing and three tiny ones on top for sensing light.
A bee's wings flap about **two hundred times every second**, which makes the buzzing sound.
Honeycomb rooms have six sides, called **hexagons**, because that shape holds the most honey using the least wax.

fact_pack.summary: Bees are flying insects living almost everywhere flowers grow, and a honeybee hive works together like one giant family. Beyond making honey, bees pollinate much of the food people eat, and scientists still study how these tiny insects talk and find their way home.

facts.text: A honeybee colony usually has one queen, tens of thousands of female worker bees, and a smaller number of male drones.
A healthy queen bee can lay up to about 2,000 eggs a day during the busy spring season.
Worker bees are all female and take turns doing every job in the hive, from cleaning cells to guarding the entrance to flying out to find flowers.
A drone's only job is to mate with a queen, and hives push drones out before winter because they cannot forage or sting to help defend the colony.
Scientists have described roughly 20,000 species of bees around the world, and only a few of them, like the honeybee, make the honey people eat.
Austrian scientist Karl von Frisch discovered that honeybees perform a 'waggle dance' to tell each other a flower's direction and distance.
Karl von Frisch won the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1973 for figuring out how bees communicate through dance and scent.
One worker honeybee makes only about a twelfth of a teaspoon of honey in her entire lifetime.
Bees in a colony together may visit roughly two million flowers to gather enough nectar to make just one pound of honey.
Because honey has very little water and is naturally acidic, sealed pots of honey found in ancient Egyptian tombs are still edible thousands of years later.
A bee has five eyes in total: two large compound eyes for seeing shapes and colors, plus three tiny simple eyes on top of its head for sensing light.
A honeybee's wings beat about 200 times every second, and that fast flapping is what makes the buzzing sound people hear.
Only female bees have a stinger, and a honeybee worker's stinger is barbed so it stays in mammal skin, which means she dies soon after she stings.
Bees and other pollinators help produce roughly one out of every three bites of food humans eat, including apples, blueberries, and almonds.
Each spring, truckloads of honeybee hives are shipped into California to pollinate its almond orchards.
Beekeepers began widely reporting Colony Collapse Disorder in 2006, when many adult worker bees mysteriously left their hives and did not return.
Researchers link colony losses to several causes together: mites, disease, pesticides, and lost flowering habitat.
Honeycomb cells are built in a six-sided hexagon shape because it lets bees store the most honey while using the least amount of wax.
On cold days bees cluster and shiver their flight muscles to keep the hive near 95°F (35°C).
Bees preserved in amber roughly 100 million years old show bees lived alongside dinosaurs.
Egyptian wall art from around 2400 BC shows beekeepers collecting honeycomb, among the oldest farming records.
A single honeybee hive can hold 20,000 to 80,000 bees at the height of summer.

Egyptian art shows people keeping bees and collecting honey
Karl von Frisch wins the Nobel Prize for decoding the bee waggle dance
Colony Collapse Disorder is first widely reported in the United States

story.title: Omar and the Bell That Remembers Every Bike
story.subtitle: A BMX kid rolls through two hundred years of wheels

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Bell in the Garage
chapters.text:
Omar spun his BMX bike in a tight circle on the driveway, trying the bunny hop he had almost landed all week. His back tire thumped down early. Not quite.

Inside the garage, something glinted on the wall. An old bike, rusty and forgotten, leaned there with a brass bell on its handlebar. Omar had never noticed it before.

He gave the bell a ring. **DING!** It flashed green and hummed like a jar of bees. **WHOOOOSH!** The garage spun away.

Omar landed on a dusty road that smelled like woodsmoke. A man in a tall hat pushed along a wooden two-wheeler with no pedals at all, running it along with his own feet.

"That's not a bike," Omar said. "It's missing the pedals!"

"This is my **Laufmaschine** — my 'running machine,'" the man said proudly. "I'm **Karl von Drais**, and in **1817** I built the very first one of these." He steered it with handlebars, just like Omar's own bike. People in town were already calling it the **hobby horse**.

Omar hopped on and pushed off with his sneakers, wobbling wildly before he found his balance. "This is basically a balance bike with no training wheels!"

"If only I'd thought of pedals," Karl sighed.

"Oh, somebody will," Omar grinned, and the bell on his wrist rang again, dragging the road into a blur.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Boneshaker Road
chapters.text:
**WHOOOOSH!** Omar landed on a street made of bumpy round stones, somewhere in France.

Two men were bolting pedals straight onto a front wheel. "Try it," said one, **Pierre Michaux**, waving Omar over. Omar climbed on and pedaled hard over the cobblestones — and nearly bit his own tongue.

"RATTLE RATTLE RATTLE!" he yelled. "This is a boneshaker!"

"That's exactly what people call it," laughed the other man, **Pierre Lallement**. "The **velocipede**. In **1866**, I even got the idea for a pedal bike officially written down as mine, in America."

Omar rubbed his teeth and looked at the wheels. Both were small. "What if the front wheel was huge? You'd go way faster for every push."

Pierre's eyebrows shot up. "Huge, you say..."

The bell on Omar's wrist buzzed, as if it liked that idea very much, and the cobblestones dissolved into mist.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Taking a Header
chapters.text:
The mist cleared on a park path. Omar's jaw dropped. A bicycle rolled past with a front wheel taller than the rider — taller than Omar's dad!

"That's the **penny-farthing**," said a passing gentleman, tipping his hat. "Named for two coins, a big **penny** and a tiny **farthing** — one huge wheel, one tiny one."

A rider up ahead hit a bump. He tipped forward, sailed clean over the handlebars, and landed in a hedge with a soft **FWUMP**. He popped up grinning, hat askew, completely fine.

"They call that **taking a header**," the gentleman said. "Happens all the time. Good thing hedges are soft."

Omar eyed the enormous front wheel. "Sitting way up there seems like a bad idea. What if both wheels were just... regular size?"

"Regular size," the gentleman repeated slowly, as though trying the words on for size.

The bell rang, pulling Omar onward before he could watch anyone else take a header.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Safe and Normal Bike
chapters.text:
Omar landed outside a workshop in England, where a man was tightening a loop of metal links around two wheels — two wheels the exact same size, low to the ground.

"Finally!" Omar said. "A bike that looks like mine!"

"I'm **John Kemp Starley**," said the man, wiping his hands. "In **1885** I built this — the **Rover Safety Bicycle**. A chain spins the back wheel, and both wheels sit low and even."

Omar hopped on and rode a slow circle. No towering wheel, no wobble, nothing scary at all. "You could do tricks on this and actually land them!"

"It caught on everywhere, fast," Starley said. "People liked not flying over the handlebars."

Omar bounced the tire with his palm. It was hard as a rock. "This part could use some work, though."

Starley scratched his head. "Funny you should say that."

The bell buzzed eagerly, and the workshop melted away.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Squishy Tire
chapters.text:
Omar landed in a yard where a man knelt beside a small tricycle, wrapping a rubbery tube around its wheel and pumping it full of air.

"I'm **John Boyd Dunlop**," the man said. "I'm a vet, but my son's tricycle rattled his teeth on every ride, so in **1888** I built this — a **pneumatic tire**, meaning it's filled with air instead of solid rubber."

Omar pressed the tire with his thumb. It squished like a cushion. "That is SO much softer."

Dunlop fitted one onto a bigger bike and let Omar take it down the garden path. The ride was smooth as butter, no rattling at all.

"This tire company is going to grow huge," Omar predicted, grinning. "People are gonna put your name on tires forever."

"Ha! We'll see," said Dunlop, though he looked pleased.

Omar squeezed the brakes, spun out a little skid for fun, and the bell chimed him away mid-slide.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Golden Age
chapters.text:
The next street was packed — bikes everywhere, bells ringing, bicycle bells jingling like a parade. A sign read it was the **1890s**, and bikes were selling by the millions across whole countries at once.

A woman zoomed past wearing puffy trouser-like pants instead of a long skirt. "Skirts get caught in the gears," she called over her shoulder. "These are called **bloomers**. Much safer for riding!"

A voice nearby, belonging to a determined-looking woman named **Susan B. Anthony**, said, "Cycling has done more to **free** women than anything else in the world — I said that myself."

Omar watched riders zip past, laughing, racing, going wherever they pleased. "You can just... go anywhere now. By yourself."

"Exactly," she said.

Omar popped a wheelie for the crowd, who cheered, and the bell on his wrist rang him onward, buzzing with approval.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Bike Shop That Learned to Fly
chapters.text:
Omar landed inside a shop smelling of oil and metal, in **Dayton, Ohio**, bike frames hanging from every wall.

Two brothers were fitting spoked wheels onto a frame. "I'm **Wilbur**," said one. "This is **Orville**," said the other. "We fix and build bicycles here in the **1890s**."

Omar noticed thin metal tubes stacked in the corner. "Those look way too light for a bike."

"Light is good," Orville said. "Light metal tubes, spoked wheels built to hold weight without being heavy — we're borrowing these same tricks for something new."

"New like what?"

Wilbur smiled a secret smile. "In **1903**, you'll see."

Omar squinted at a sketch on the workbench — it had wings. "No way. You're gonna FLY?"

Neither brother answered, just kept tightening spokes, humming, while the bell on Omar's wrist buzzed with excitement, like it already knew.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Back to the Garage
chapters.text:
The bell rang twice, fast, and dragged Omar through a blur of bikes: riders shifting little levers to climb hills easily with **gears** that arrived in the **1930s**; a long, long race called the **Tour de France**, started in **1903**, stretching about **3,500 kilometers** across France; kids doing jumps on small tough **BMX bikes** in the **1970s**; riders bumping down dirt trails on wide-tired **mountain bikes**, built the same decade in California.

Then, **WHOOOOSH** — the garage again, dusty and quiet, Omar's own BMX bike waiting on the driveway outside.

The old bell on the wall had gone still and silver, no more green glow. But something sat on the handlebar grip that hadn't been there before — a tiny silver gear charm, no bigger than a coin.

Omar closed his fist around it and grinned at his bike. Somewhere out there, right now, more than a **billion** bikes were rolling — more than any other kind of vehicle on Earth. And one of them was his.

He wheeled it inside, parked it by the old bike, and gave both bells one last, gentle ring.

true_facts.text: In **1817**, **Karl von Drais** built a wooden two-wheeler with no pedals, pushed along with the feet, nicknamed the **hobby horse**.
It was steered with handlebars, just like bikes today.
In the 1860s, pedals were bolted straight onto the front wheel, making the **velocipede**, nicknamed the **boneshaker** for its bumpy ride.
In **1866**, **Pierre Lallement** got his pedal bike idea officially recognized as his own in America.
In the 1870s, the **penny-farthing** had a giant front wheel and a tiny back wheel.
It was named after two old coins, one big and one tiny.
Riding one was risky — a sudden stop could send the rider flying forward, called **taking a header**.
In **1885**, **John Kemp Starley** built the **Rover Safety Bicycle**, with two even wheels and a chain, much safer to ride.
In **1888**, **John Boyd Dunlop** invented the air-filled **pneumatic tire** for his son's tricycle, making rides much smoother.
In the 1890s, bike riding became a huge craze, with millions of bikes sold across whole countries.
**Susan B. Anthony** said cycling freed women more than almost anything else, since bikes let them go places on their own.
Long skirts were dangerous around bike gears, so riders started wearing **bloomers** instead.
**Wilbur and Orville Wright** ran a bicycle shop in **Dayton, Ohio** in the 1890s before building the first airplane in **1903**.
Today there are more than a **billion** bicycles in the world — more than any other kind of vehicle.

fact_pack.summary: Bicycles evolved over 200 years from a wooden walking machine with no pedals to today's lightweight, geared bikes ridden by billions of people. Along the way inventors added pedals, chains, air-filled tires, and gears, making bikes faster, safer, and more comfortable.

facts.text: In 1817, German inventor Karl von Drais built the 'Laufmaschine' or 'running machine,' a wooden two-wheeler with no pedals that riders pushed along with their feet.
Von Drais's invention was nicknamed the 'draisine' or 'hobby horse' and was steered with handlebars, much like a modern bike.

In the 1860s, French makers Pierre Michaux and Pierre Lallement added pedals directly to the front wheel, creating the 'velocipede,' nicknamed the 'boneshaker' for its rough ride on cobblestone streets.
Pierre Lallement patented a pedal-driven bicycle design in the United States in 1866.
In the 1870s, the 'penny-farthing' bicycle appeared, with a giant front wheel (sometimes taller than a person) and a tiny back wheel, letting riders go faster with one pedal turn.
Penny-farthings were named after two British coins of very different sizes, the large penny and the small farthing.
Riding a penny-farthing was risky because the rider sat high above the front wheel and could be thrown headfirst in a sudden stop, a fall nicknamed 'taking a header.'
In 1885, Englishman John Kemp Starley invented the 'Rover Safety Bicycle,' with two similarly sized wheels and a chain driving the back wheel, much closer to modern bikes.
The safety bicycle's lower, even wheels made it much easier and safer to ride than the penny-farthing, and it quickly became the standard design worldwide.
In 1888, Scottish inventor John Boyd Dunlop developed the practical pneumatic (air-filled) rubber tire, making bike rides much smoother than solid rubber tires.
Dunlop's tire company grew into the Dunlop Tyre brand, still famous today for tires on bikes and cars.
The 1890s bicycle craze, called the 'Golden Age of Bicycles,' saw millions of bikes sold across Europe and the United States.
Bicycles gave women new freedom to travel independently in the 1890s, and American reformer Susan B. Anthony said cycling 'has done more to emancipate women than anything else in the world.'
Because long skirts were dangerous around bike gears and wheels, the bicycle craze helped popularize more practical clothing for women, including bloomers.
Wilbur and Orville Wright, who later invented the first successful airplane in 1903, ran a bicycle repair and manufacturing shop in Dayton, Ohio in the 1890s.
The Wright brothers used bicycle-building skills, like lightweight metal tubing and spoked wheels, to help design their early flying machines.
Multi-speed gear systems, called derailleurs, became common on bikes in the 1930s, letting riders shift gears to handle hills more easily.
The Tour de France, the world's most famous long-distance cycling race, began in 1903 and today covers about 3,500 kilometers (2,175 miles) across France over about three weeks.
BMX bikes, small and sturdy for tricks and dirt racing, became popular in the United States in the 1970s, inspired by motocross motorcycles.
Mountain bikes with wide, knobby tires were developed in the 1970s in Marin County, California, by riders who wanted to bike down rough dirt trails.
Today, an estimated one billion or more bicycles exist worldwide, more than any other kind of vehicle.
The Netherlands and Denmark are famous today for having more bicycles than cars in some cities, with wide bike lanes built for everyday cyclists.
Modern bicycles are made from lightweight materials like aluminum and carbon fiber, letting racing bikes weigh less than 8 kilograms (about 17 pounds).

story.title: Sam and Sticky's Sticky-Toe Adventure
story.subtitle: A climb-every-wall tour with a gecko named Sticky

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: Sticky Wakes Up
chapters.text:
Sam sat cross-legged on his bedroom floor. A jar of roly-polies sat beside him. One shiny black beetle tapped at the glass, trying to get out.

Sam loved bugs. He picked up every single bug in the garden, even the squirmy, wiggly ones.

On his shelf sat a small rubber gecko. His name was Sticky. Sam had had him since he was a baby.

Tonight, something strange happened. Sticky's eyes blinked. They glowed bright green.

"Sam," said a tiny voice. "Want to see how real geckos climb walls?"

Sam's mouth fell open. "YES!"

Sticky hopped off the shelf. He started to grow. Soon he was as big as a puppy, with warm, bumpy skin.

"Hop on," Sticky said.

There was a WHOOSH of green light. Sam shrank down, down, down, tiny as a ladybug.

They landed on a tall, cool window. A real gecko walked straight up the glass. He even walked upside down, easy as pie.

"How does he stick?" Sam asked, leaning close.

"Look at his toes," said Sticky.

Sam squinted. Each toe was covered in millions of tiny hairs. Too small to see on their own.

"Those are called **setae**," said Sticky. "Each one splits into even tinier tips. They hold on with a gentle, sticky pull. Not glue. Just a soft, cozy grip."

"Like a hug?" Sam asked.

"Just like a hug," said Sticky.

"Does he get stuck forever?" Sam asked.

"Watch," said Sticky.

The gecko peeled one toe up. Then another. PEEL, PEEL, PEEL, like pulling up tape. Off he walked, clean as can be.

"And look," said Sticky. "Dirt just rolls right off his feet while he walks. His toes never get yucky."

Sam clapped his hands. "No glue, no mess! That's the best trick ever!"

Sticky grinned. "Climb high, climb smart, Sam."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Spider on the Glass
chapters.text:
A silky thread shimmered near Sam's foot. He looked up. A spider was climbing that very same window, leg over leg.

"Spiders!" Sam said. "My favorite!"

"Watch her feet," said Sticky.

Sam leaned in close, careful not to touch her, just the way his mom always told him with bugs outside.

Her legs were covered in tiny hairs too, just like the gecko's toes.

"Those hairs have a name as well," said Sticky. "Thousands of tiny hairs called **setules**. They work kind of like gecko hair. That's why lots of spiders can climb right up glass."

"She's doing the gecko trick!" Sam said.

He counted her legs, pointing at each one. "One, two, three... eight!"

The spider reached the top of the window and tucked herself into a corner, safe and snug.

"Good counting," said Sticky.

Sam waved at her. "Nice climbing, spider!"

He did not touch her. He just watched, same as always.

"I always wondered how spiders did that," Sam said. "Now I know their secret."

Sticky chuckled. "One mystery down. Lots more to go tonight."

Sam bounced on his toes. "What's next?"

Something buzzed past their heads. BZZZZZ.

"That," said Sticky, pointing, "is next."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Fly's Sticky Secret
chapters.text:
BZZZZZ. A fat fly landed on the glass right beside them.

Sam giggled. "Whoa, he's walking upside down too!"

"Watch his feet," said Sticky.

Sam got close. Tiny pads on the fly's feet squished down with each step. A little drop of goo came out every time.

"Ew! Is that glue?" Sam asked, scrunching up his nose.

"Almost," said Sticky. "Flies climb using tiny foot pads that ooze a sticky liquid. It's like their own homemade glue."

"Sticky feet, just like your name!" Sam said, poking Sticky's arm.

"Exactly like my name," Sticky said, laughing so hard his tail wiggled.

The fly took off. BZZZZ. It landed on the ceiling, upside down, without falling even a little.

Sam looked amazed. "He never falls!"

"Because of his gluey feet," said Sticky.

Sam thought for a second, tapping his chin. "Spiders have hairs. Geckos have hairs. Flies have goo. Everybody's got a different trick!"

"Now you're really getting it," said Sticky, giving Sam a gentle high-five.

Sam wiped his hand on his pajama pants, just in case any goo had rubbed off. It hadn't. He laughed at himself anyway.

"What sticks next?" Sam asked.

Sticky pointed down at the garden below. "Ants. Lots and lots of ants."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Ants, Claws, and Sticky Feet
chapters.text:
They zoomed down to the garden path. Tiny ants marched along a rough stone wall, not slipping once.

"How come he doesn't fall?" Sam asked, pointing at one busy ant.

"Ants use two different tools," said Sticky. "Sharp little claws for rough walls, like this stone. Sticky pads for smooth walls, like glass."

Sam spotted a shiny tile near the garden gate. "What happens if he climbs that one?"

"Let's find out," said Sticky.

An ant wandered onto the smooth tile. It switched from claws to soft, sticky pads, gluing down each tiny step.

"He changed his shoes!" Sam shouted.

"Sort of," Sticky laughed. "He just used a different tool for a different job."

A cockroach scuttled by a moment later, doing the very same trick. Claws on the rough stone. Sticky pads on the smooth tile.

Sam grinned. "Everybody's got more than one trick up their sleeve!"

"Just like you," said Sticky. "You scoop up beetles one way and watch spiders another way, don't you?"

Sam nodded. "Beetles I scoop gently. Spiders I just watch."

"Smart bug-catcher," said Sticky, bumping Sam's fist with one scaly hand.

Sam looked at the busy little ants, marching on and on. "They never even stop to rest!"

"Nope," said Sticky. "Too busy climbing."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Up the Goat Mountain
chapters.text:
WHOOSH. Green light swirled again. This time, they landed on a rocky, steep cliff. Sam gulped, just a little. It looked awfully high up.

"Don't worry," said Sticky right away. "Nobody's going to fall. Just look."

A mountain goat stood on a tiny ledge of rock, calm as could be.

"How does he stay up there?" Sam asked, feeling braver already.

"Look at his hooves," said Sticky.

Sam peeked. Each hoof had a hard outer edge and a soft, squishy middle part.

"The hard edge grips the rock," said Sticky. "The soft middle squishes and molds around the bumps, like a bendy puzzle piece."

The goat hopped from rock to rock, never slipping once, not even close.

"He's like a mountain ninja!" Sam said.

Sticky laughed so hard he wobbled. "A mountain ninja. I like that one."

Sam's little wobble of worry melted clean away. The goat looked happy up there, not scared at all.

"Can geckos climb rocks like that too?" Sam asked.

"Different job, different feet," said Sticky. "Gecko feet are best for smooth walls. Goat hooves are best for bumpy rocks."

Sam nodded slowly, thinking hard. "Everybody picks their own best tool."

"Now you sound like a real scientist," said Sticky, patting Sam's head gently.

Sam puffed out his chest, proud as anything.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Squirrel's Tiny Claws
chapters.text:
A flash of fur zipped past them. A squirrel raced straight up a tall tree trunk, quick as a blink.

"Whoa, he's fast!" Sam said.

"Look closely," said Sticky.

Sam squinted at the squirrel's tiny feet. Sharp, curved claws dug right into the bark.

"The bark looks smooth from far away," said Sticky. "But it has tiny bumps and cracks too small for us to see. His claws grab right onto them."

Sam reached out and touched the tree trunk, not the squirrel, just the bark. "Whoa, it's bumpy!" he said. "I never noticed that before."

"Now you've got squirrel eyes," said Sticky, grinning.

The squirrel paused on a branch, flicked its tail, and zoomed even higher.

Sam laughed. "Bye, speedy squirrel! Thanks for the tour!"

"Claws for bark, hairs for glass, goo for flies, hooves for rock," Sticky counted on his fingers, one by one. "Lots of different tricks for lots of different walls."

Sam counted on his own fingers too, very seriously. "Four tricks so far!"

"Two more to go," said Sticky, pointing toward a pond glittering in the dark. "And these two are extra squishy."

Sam giggled. "Squishy is my favorite kind of trick."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Frog Toes and Snail Trails
chapters.text:
They landed near a pond. Rain had just fallen, and every leaf glistened under the moon.

A tiny tree frog hopped onto a wet leaf and stuck there, easy as anything.

"How does he stick to something so wet?" Sam asked.

"His toes are flat and a little slippery-slimy," said Sticky. "Tiny patterns shaped like little honeycomb circles help him grip, even on wet leaves and glass."

"Honeycomb, like the bees make!" Sam said.

"Just like that," said Sticky.

Nearby, a snail glided slowly up a smooth rock. Sam watched its soft, squishy foot ripple in little waves, back and forth.

"He's so slow!" Sam said, trying not to giggle too loud.

"He's climbing on slime," said Sticky. "It lets his soft foot grip the rock, little wave by little wave."

Sam watched the snail's shiny trail glisten behind it in the moonlight. "He leaves a sparkly road!"

"He sure does," said Sticky.

Sam clapped both hands together. "Frog sticks with slimy toes. Snail sticks with a slime trail. So many tricks tonight!"

"Six tricks now," said Sticky, counting them all off. "Pretty amazing, huh?"

Sam nodded hard, his hair flopping. "The best night ever!"

He gave the frog a tiny wave, and the snail an even tinier one. He did not touch either of them. He just watched, happy as could be.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Home Again
chapters.text:
WHOOSH. Green light swirled around them once more.

Sam landed back on his bedroom floor with a soft PLOP. His jar of roly-polies sat right where he left it, lid still on tight.

Sticky shrank back down to his regular rubber-gecko size, right back onto the shelf where he belonged.

Sam looked down at his own fingers. "I didn't touch a single spider, or a frog, or a snail," he said proudly. "I just watched, like Mom always tells me."

"Best kind of bug-catcher there is," said Sticky, his green glow fading to a soft, sleepy twinkle.

On the windowsill, Sam spotted something new. A tiny gold sticker, shaped just like a gecko's footprint, sparkling in the moonlight.

"Is that from tonight?" Sam asked, picking it up carefully.

"A little souvenir," said Sticky. "So you remember every sticky, clawy, slimy trick we saw."

Sam pressed the sticker gently onto the side of his bug jar. "Now my jar can climb walls too," he said, grinning.

Sticky chuckled one last, sleepy chuckle. "Climb high, climb smart, Sam."

Sam yawned a giant yawn and crawled under his covers, thinking about hairy toes, gluey feet, hard hooves, and sparkly snail trails, all the way to sleep.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Sam. Climb high, climb smart.

fact_pack.summary: Lots of animals can climb smooth walls and even walk upside down on ceilings, using clever tricks like sticky pads, tiny hooked claws, or millions of microscopic hairs. Scientists who study these tricks have even copied them to invent new kinds of sticky tape and climbing gloves for people.

facts.text: Geckos can run up glass and walk across ceilings because their toes have millions of microscopic hairs called setae.
Each gecko seta splits into hundreds of even tinier tips called spatulae, which get so close to a surface that weak molecular attractions called van der Waals forces hold the foot in place.
A gecko's sticky grip is not glue, so its feet never get messy or leave residue, and it can lift its toes off instantly by peeling them, toe by toe, like pulling up tape.
Flies and some beetles climb using tiny pads on their feet that ooze a sticky liquid, acting like natural glue drops.
Spiders have thousands of microscopic hairs called setules on their feet, similar in idea to gecko hairs, which is why many spiders can climb smooth glass.
Ants and cockroaches use a combination of sharp claws for rough surfaces and sticky footpads for smooth ones, switching tools depending on the wall.
Mountain goats and some wild sheep climb near-vertical cliffs using hooves with a hard outer rim and a soft, grippy inner pad that molds to rock.
Squirrels climb trees and walls using sharp curved claws that dig into tiny cracks and bumps invisible to human eyes.
Tree frogs have special flattened, mucus-covered toe pads with tiny hexagon-shaped patterns that help them stick to wet leaves and glass.
Snails and slugs climb smooth walls by gliding on a layer of slime, which lets their muscular foot grip and move in rippling waves.
Some crabs and lobsters use small hooked bristles on their legs to cling to rocky, underwater walls against strong currents.
Bats cannot climb walls quickly like geckos, but they use curved claws on their feet to hang upside down from cave ceilings and cliff walls.
Woodpeckers climb straight up tree trunks using stiff tail feathers as a prop and two toes forward, two toes back for extra grip.
In 2014, scientists built a gecko-inspired handheld paddle that let a person climb a glass wall by pressing sticky synthetic pads against it.
Engineers have copied gecko foot structure to create reusable sticky tape and gripping robot feet that work in space, where regular glue fails in a vacuum.
A gecko's sticking ability is so strong that scientists calculated a gecko the size of a human could theoretically support its whole body weight from one finger, though real geckos are small.
Geckos keep their sticky feet clean and dust-free through a self-cleaning effect, where dirt particles roll off the tiny hairs as the gecko walks.
Praying mantises and stick insects use both small claws and sticky pads called arolia, choosing which one to use depending on the surface.
Some climbing animals, like certain ants, are so light compared to their sticky footpad area that they could theoretically hold many times their own body weight while hanging upside down.
Rock climbers sometimes study gecko and insect feet for ideas on new types of climbing shoes and gloves with better grip.
Many wall-climbing animals rely on physics tricks rather than suction, since true suction cups need airless pockets that are hard to maintain on rough or dusty surfaces.
Remoras, a type of fish, use a modified dorsal fin shaped like a suction pad to stick to sharks, whales, and boat hulls rather than walls.

story.title: Milo and Juno and the Brick That Glowed
story.subtitle: A sparkly, clicky trip through the real history of LEGO

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Brick That Glowed
chapters.text:
Milo built a shark out of red and gray LEGO bricks. Its teeth were tiny white triangles.

Juno stacked green bricks into a dinosaur. It had a long neck and two stompy feet.

Then one old brick on the carpet started to glow. It glowed soft green, like a firefly.

"Whoa," said Milo. He picked it up. It felt warm.

CLICK! The brick popped open. Out hopped a tiny LEGO man, no bigger than Milo's thumb.

"Hello! I'm Clicky," he said. "I live inside bricks."

Juno giggled. "You're so small!"

"Small, but mighty," said Clicky. "Want to see where LEGO bricks come from? Hold my hand."

WHOOOSH! The room spun like a tornado made of bricks. Then it stopped.

They stood in a wooden workshop. Curly wood shavings covered the floor. A kind-faced man was carving a toy duck.

"That's Ole Kirk Christiansen," whispered Clicky. "In 1932, he started a little company in a town called Billund, in Denmark. First he made wooden toys and ladders."

Milo looked around. "No LEGO bricks yet?"

"Not yet," said Clicky. "But just wait."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Play Well
chapters.text:
Ole Kirk hung a new sign over his workshop door. Milo read the letters out loud. "L-E-G-O."

"What does that mean?" asked Juno.

"In 1934, Ole Kirk took two Danish words, leg godt," said Clicky. "They mean play well. He squished them together to make LEGO."

Milo grinned. "Play well. I like that."

"Here's a funny bit," said Clicky. "Some people say lego also means I put together in an old language called Latin. That's probably just a happy accident, not the real reason. Still fun to know."

Juno tried saying it. "Lay-go. Play well!"

Ole Kirk waved from his doorway, proud of his new sign.

"Can we help build something?" asked Milo.

"Not yet," said Clicky. "Something squishy and shiny is coming first."

Milo's eyes went wide. "Squishy?"

"You'll see," said Clicky, tugging their hands. WHOOOSH!

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Squishy Shiny Machine
chapters.text:
They landed with a soft THUD in a bigger workshop. A giant metal machine stood in the corner, humming.

"What's that?" asked Milo.

"In 1947, Ole Kirk got one of the first plastic machines in Denmark," said Clicky. "It's called an injection molding machine. Big name, simple job. It melts plastic, then squeezes it into a shape, like squirting toothpaste into a toy mold."

SPLOOSH! Hot plastic oozed into a brick-shaped mold.

Juno pointed. "It's making a brick!"

Milo pressed his hands together like a mold. "Squeeze, squeeze, squeeze!"

The machine chugged and clanked. Out popped a shiny plastic brick. Everyone cheered.

"It's warm!" said Milo, holding it gently.

"Careful. Let it cool," said Clicky.

They waited. Then Milo held the cooled brick up like a trophy.

"First plastic brick ever," said Clicky. "It doesn't click yet, though. That part comes later."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Wobbly Bricks
chapters.text:
Years rolled by in a blink. Clicky led them to a table of bumpy plastic bricks.

"In 1949, these were called Automatic Binding Bricks," said Clicky. "They're hollow underneath, like little cups. And they have bumps on top."

Juno stacked three bricks into a tower. She tapped it. It wobbled. Then it tipped. CLATTER!

"Oops," said Juno, giggling instead of being upset.

"They stack," said Clicky, "but they don't hold tight yet."

Milo flipped a brick over and peeked underneath. "Why don't they stick?"

"Very good question," said Clicky. "Somebody is about to fix that."

Juno tried stacking again, slower this time. Still wobbly. "Silly bricks," she laughed.

"Don't worry," said Clicky. "The best part is coming. Hold tight." WHOOOSH!

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Tubes That Click
chapters.text:
They landed in a workshop covered in drawings. A man flipped a brick over and over, frowning at its empty bottom.

"That's Godtfred," whispered Clicky. "Ole Kirk's son."

Milo peeked at the hollow brick too. "What if something was inside here," he said, "to grab the bumps on the brick below?"

Godtfred looked up, surprised. Then he grinned and grabbed a pencil. He drew little round tubes inside the brick's bottom.

"In 1958, Godtfred's new brick got its own special paper, called a patent," said Clicky. "That paper says it's a brand new invention."

Juno pressed two new bricks together. CLICK! She pulled. It held tight.

"IT CLICKS!" shouted Milo.

"Here's the amazing part," said Clicky. "A brick made in 1958 still clicks with a brick made today. The tubes barely changed at all."

Milo pictured his shark at home. "So my bricks would click with this one?"

"Exactly," said Clicky.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Bricks That Stay Bright
chapters.text:
The workshop faded. They stood in a sunny room full of colorful bricks: red, yellow, blue, green.

"In 1963, LEGO started using a tougher plastic called ABS," said Clicky. "It doesn't crack easily. The colors stay bright for a very long time."

Milo held an old red brick next to a brand new one. "They're the same red!"

"That's the idea," said Clicky.

Juno sniffed a brick. "Smells like... nothing."

"Good," laughed Clicky. "It's not supposed to smell like anything."

Milo stacked ten bricks, his tallest tower ever. It didn't wobble one bit.

"Ten bricks high!" he cheered.

Juno added one more. Eleven! She did a little victory dance.

"Steady hands," said Clicky. "You two would make great brick builders."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: A Park Made of Bricks
chapters.text:
WHOOOSH! They landed outside, in bright sunshine. Big LEGO models stood everywhere: a castle, a dragon, a tiny town.

"In 1968, the very first LEGOLAND park opened, right in Billund," said Clicky. "It's full of models built from LEGO bricks, right next to the first factory."

Juno gasped at a huge brick dinosaur. "It's MY size... no, bigger!"

"Even bigger," said Milo, counting windows on the brick castle.

Clicky held out two bigger, chunkier bricks. "In 1969, LEGO made special big bricks for little builders. They're called DUPLO. Easier for small hands. And they still click with regular LEGO bricks too."

Juno grabbed one happily. "Finally, bricks my size!"

She clicked a DUPLO brick onto Milo's smaller one. It fit.

"See?" said Clicky. "Big or small, they all play well together."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Gears and Little People
chapters.text:
Next stop: a table full of gears, wheels, and tiny plastic people with yellow faces.

"In 1977, LEGO added gears and axles for building machines," said Clicky. "That line is called Technic."

Milo spun a gear with his finger. It turned three other gears. "Whoa, they're all connected!"

Then Clicky picked up a tiny figure. It had bendy arms and a hat that popped off.

"In 1978, the first LEGO minifigures appeared," said Clicky. "You can swap their heads, their hats, even give one a shark hat."

Milo laughed and put a tiny shark fin on the figure's head. "A LEGO shark person!"

Juno asked, "Did a kid ever get to be in charge of LEGO?"

"Not quite a kid," said Clicky. "But in 1979, Ole Kirk's grandson Kjeld took charge of the whole company. He grew up playing with these very bricks."

Juno nodded seriously. "That's a good job."

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Back on the Carpet
chapters.text:
"One more quick peek," said Clicky, and the room shimmered.

They saw a giant screen with LEGO spaceships zooming by. "In 1999, LEGO made its first Star Wars sets," said Clicky. "And in 2014, a whole LEGO Movie played in theaters everywhere."

Juno clapped. "Bricks that are ALSO a movie?"

"Bricks can be almost anything," said Clicky.

Then WHOOOSH, softer this time, like a gentle breeze.

Milo and Juno landed back on their own bedroom carpet. The shark and the dinosaur were still there, waiting.

Clicky shrank down and hopped back into the glowing brick. "Thanks for playing well with me," he said, his voice getting tiny. "I'll be right here, whenever you need me."

The brick gave one last soft glow, then went quiet, sitting on the carpet like any other brick.

Milo tucked it carefully onto his shelf, right beside his LEGO shark.

"Goodnight, little brick," he whispered.

Juno yawned a dinosaur-sized yawn.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Milo. Goodnight, Juno. Play well.

story.title: Isla and the Secret Under the Ash
story.subtitle: One stone, one stubborn question, and an entire buried city.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Stone That Hummed
chapters.text:
Isla's bedroom wall was covered in string.

Red string, to be exact, pinned between index cards that said things like *WHO BUILT STONEHENGE?* and *WHERE DID THE MAYA GO?* Her favorite mysteries were the ones nobody had fully solved, and tonight's new card said simply: **POMPEII**. Underneath it she'd pinned a photo from a library book — a city frozen mid-sentence, streets empty, a volcano looming behind it like it was still thinking about something.

On her desk sat the one object that didn't fit the detective theme: a smooth gray stone, spiral-ridged, that her aunt had mailed her from a dig site with a note that said *found this and thought of you.* Isla rubbed it when she was thinking hard, which was most of the time.

Tonight, the stone was warm. Not pocket-warm. Warm like it had been sitting in sunlight, except her room was dark and the window was shut.

She pressed it flat against the Pompeii photo, mostly as a joke — and the photo didn't just light up, it opened. Ash-colored dust rolled off the corkboard like fog off a lake, and before she could decide whether to be amazed or alarmed, Isla was standing on a sunlit stone street, market stalls humming around her, a city rising on every side.

"Okay," she said out loud, to nobody. "New record for weirdest Tuesday."

The stone hummed twice in her closed fist, a soft questioning sound, and words seemed to arrange themselves in the dust at her feet, as if someone were writing with a stick: *Pompeii. A real town. Go look.*

Isla looked. The town was busy — really busy, carts rattling, voices arguing over the price of fish, somebody laughing two streets over. This wasn't a ruin. This was **Pompeii** before anything happened to it, a lively Roman town near where the Italian city of Naples stands today, home to somewhere between **11,000 and 15,000 people** — shoppers, bathers, actors, worshippers, all going about an entirely normal day.

A boy selling bread rolls shouted a name across the street that Isla almost recognized. She tugged the stone, and it hummed again, translating without quite explaining how. "Why is it called Pompeii?" she murmured.

The dust-letters rearranged themselves: *pompe. An old word here. Means 'five.'* Isla grinned — she loved a name with a hidden story. Maybe, the stone seemed to suggest, five small villages had once joined together to make one town, and the name stuck around long after anyone remembered why.

"A whole city's name is basically a fossil of five arguments that got solved," Isla said. She liked that. She filed it under *case notes* in her head and kept walking, because something about this town — alive, loud, completely unaware — made her stomach do a small, nervous flip she didn't yet have words for.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Gaps in the Street
chapters.text:
The street under Isla's sneakers wasn't flat. It was made of big paving stones with tall stepping stones set across it in rows, like someone had built a crosswalk out of boulders.

She stopped to study them, because a mystery she could actually examine was Isla's favorite kind. "Why would you put rocks in the middle of a road?" she asked the stone in her fist.

It hummed, patient. A cart rattled past at that exact moment — and rolled straight through a gap between the stepping stones, wheels fitting the space perfectly, while a woman crossed the road dry-footed by hopping stone to stone above a trickle of water and muck.

"Oh!" Isla said. "It's not random. It's — it's a system." **Pompeii's streets had raised stepping stones** so people could cross without wading through mud or water, while carts still rolled through the gaps underneath, wheels straddling the stones like a car driving over a curb cut. Someone here had solved a problem Isla's own street still hadn't: how to keep people's feet dry *and* let traffic through.

She followed the water with her eyes and found where it came from — a stone fountain on the corner, water gushing steadily from a carved spout, with pipes running off beneath the street. Isla crouched to look. "Are those—"

*Lead pipes,* the dust spelled out. *Bringing water to the whole town.*

**Pompeii had an advanced water system**, fountains on nearly every corner, with pipes carrying water in from outside the walls so that nobody had to haul buckets from a well. Isla thought about her own house, where water simply appeared out of a tap, and realized she'd never once wondered how that miracle worked. Two thousand years ago, somebody in this town had already wondered, and built an answer.

She was crouched by the fountain, tracing a pipe with her finger, when the ground gave a short, low shudder — barely anything, gone almost as soon as it started. A market stall's pots rattled. A man steadied his cart and kept walking without even glancing down, like it happened all the time.

"Was that an earthquake?" Isla asked, standing fast.

The stone hummed low, almost thoughtful. *This town knows earthquakes,* it seemed to say. *It's had them before.* Isla filed that away too, the way a detective files a clue that doesn't make sense yet: a small shake, shrugged off by everyone who lived here, in a town sitting at the foot of a mountain nobody in the street was even looking at.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Oval in the Ground
chapters.text:
A roar went up ahead of Isla — not a scary roar, a *stadium* roar, thousands of voices cheering at once.

She followed it around a corner and stopped dead. In front of her sat an enormous oval building, stone benches rising in rings around a sandy floor, packed with people leaning forward, yelling, laughing, pointing.

"That's an amphitheater," Isla said slowly, pleased with herself for knowing the word — a big oval arena built for watching shows, kind of like an ancient stadium. "But that's — that's really old for one of these, isn't it?"

The stone warmed against her palm. *Built around 70 BC,* the dust spelled. *One of the oldest ever found.*

Isla did the math in her head and whistled. **Pompeii's amphitheater was built around 70 BC**, which meant it was already ancient history even to the people cheering in it that very afternoon — built for watching gladiator games, the dramatic contests Roman crowds loved best. She climbed partway up an empty section of bench to get a better look, and the whole bowl of noise and sunburned shoulders and waving arms opened up below her.

"It's basically a two-thousand-year-old soccer stadium," she muttered, filing another note. "Except gladiators instead of penalty kicks."

A family nearby had brought snacks wrapped in cloth and were arguing cheerfully about who had the best seats, exactly like Isla's own family did at school assemblies. That was the part that kept surprising her: not that Pompeii was ancient, but that it was *normal.* People complaining about seat views. People showing up late. People just — living.

On her way back down the steps, she noticed words painted in red on the outside wall of a building across the street, bold and blocky like a campaign poster. She couldn't read the Latin, but the stone hummed a translation anyway: a man's name, and underneath it, a line urging everyone to vote for him.

"Wait — is that an advertisement?" Isla said, delighted. **Some Pompeii buildings had political slogans and ads painted right on the outside walls** — an ancient, sun-bleached version of a campaign sign stapled to a telephone pole, or a billboard shouting about the world's best pizza. Someone here had been running for office the exact same way people did now, just louder, and in red paint that would somehow outlast empires.

Isla laughed out loud, and for a second she almost forgot the small worried knot still sitting in her stomach from the shaking street.
chapters.shout_line: TWO THOUSAND YEARS AND THEY STILL HAD CAMPAIGN SIGNS!

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Watcher Across the Water
chapters.text:
The stone tugged her — actually tugged, a definite pull in her palm — away from the noise of the amphitheater and toward the edge of the bay, where the water lay flat and blue and a young man sat on a wall with a wax tablet balanced on his knee, writing fast.

"Who's that?" Isla whispered.

*Pliny the Younger,* the dust spelled. *Watching. Writing it all down.*

Isla edged closer, careful not to disturb him, and followed his gaze across the water to the mountain that loomed behind the whole town — Vesuvius, though nobody she'd met today had said the name like it mattered. Pliny's pen scratched steadily. He wasn't just scribbling. He was *reporting,* the way Isla took case notes, getting every detail down exactly as it happened rather than guessing at it later.

"He's basically a journalist," Isla said, impressed despite herself.

The stone hummed agreement. **A Roman writer named Pliny the Younger watched an eruption from across the bay and wrote two detailed letters describing exactly what he saw** — so careful and exact that, centuries later, scientists studying this *kind* of violent, fast, sky-darkening volcanic eruption would name it after him: a **Plinian eruption**, in his honor, just for writing it down so well that people two thousand years later could still picture it.

"Wait," Isla said, the knot in her stomach pulling tighter. "An eruption. This mountain erupts?"

*It did once,* the stone answered. *It still could. Scientists watch it closely even now.* **Mount Vesuvius is still an active volcano today**, and because so many people live near it, scientists keep a close eye on it all the time, the way a lifeguard never really stops scanning the water even on a calm day.

Isla looked at the mountain again, and this time it didn't look like scenery. It looked like a clue she'd been walking past all afternoon.

Out on the water, she spotted ships — not fishing boats, proper Roman navy ships, turning and heading *toward* the mountain instead of away from it. "Those are going the wrong way," she said.

The stone hummed low, almost proud. A commander named Pliny the Elder — an older relative of the writer on the wall, a brave man who studied nature for a living — was sailing straight toward the danger, not away from it, because he wanted to get a closer look and help anyone he could. Isla watched the ships grow smaller against the dark smudge now rising behind the mountain's peak, and understood, all at once, that the normal, busy, campaign-sign-covered town behind her had run out of normal afternoons.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: What the Sky Did
chapters.text:
The sky changed before the sound did.

One moment it was blue. The next, a column of ash was climbing straight up from the mountain's top, fast, dark, and so tall Isla had to tip her whole head back to find where it stopped — except it didn't stop, it just kept going, spreading out at the top like a mushroom made of smoke.

"That's the eruption," Isla said, very quietly. An **eruption** was simply a volcano exploding — pushing ash and broken rock up into the sky all at once, the way a shaken soda bursts out when you finally open it, except on a scale that blotted out the sun.

The stone pulled her backward, gently but firmly, away from the street and up to a safe rise of ground, the way a grown-up's hand pulls you back from a curb. Isla understood: she was watching this happen, not living through it.

From up here, safe, she watched gray-white flakes begin to fall over the rooftops below — not like snow exactly, more like dry, light little stones, bouncing off tile roofs with a soft patter. **On August 24, 79 AD, Mount Vesuvius erupted and began burying the town below in ash and light, bubbly volcanic rock called pumice.** It kept falling, hour after hour, settling into streets, piling against walls, filling courtyards, until entire rooftops simply vanished under it.

Isla pressed the stone tight in her fist. "What happens to everyone?" she asked, and her voice came out smaller than she meant it to.

The stone hummed, low and steady, the way a hand might rest on a shoulder. *Many people got away, down the coast, across the bay, before it was done,* it told her gently. *Some did not. This is a true and sad part of the story, and it belongs to them, not to a show.* It didn't say more than that, and Isla understood the stone wasn't hiding anything from her — it was simply refusing to turn real people's worst day into a spectacle, which struck her as exactly right.

By the time the ash finally stopped falling, the mountain had buried the whole town under **as much as four to six meters of ash and rock** — that's thirteen to twenty feet, deeper than Isla's entire house was tall, stacked straight down on top of every street, every fountain, every amphitheater seat.

Isla stood very still, watching gray drifts bury a town she'd been laughing in an hour before. "It's gone," she whispered.

*Not gone,* the stone corrected, humming warmer now, almost encouraging. *Hidden. There's a difference.* Isla, who had spent her whole life loving the difference between *gone* and *hidden*, felt the knot in her stomach loosen just slightly, replaced by something that felt almost like hope.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Loaf in the Oven
chapters.text:
The dust around Isla's shoes swirled and settled, and when it cleared, the ash-covered town was gone — not buried-gone, but *time-skipped* gone, replaced by a quiet dig site with canvas tents, soft brushes, and careful hands working at the ground.

She was standing in the middle of an excavation — people gently brushing centuries of ash away from walls that still had their paint on them.

"It's all just... still here," Isla breathed, crouching beside a wall where red and yellow paint curled into a picture of a leaping deer, bright as the day it was painted. **The eruption happened so fast that it froze the whole town in time**, preserving paintings on walls, writing scratched into stone by bored Romans centuries ago, and — a woman nearby was just lifting something small and round out of a stone oven with careful tongs.

Isla leaned in. "Is that—"

"Bread," the woman said, though Isla suspected it was the stone translating again. **A loaf of bread was found still sitting in a Pompeii oven, perfectly shaped, with a maker's mark still pressed into its crust** — the same mark a baker would have stamped on it before selling it, just so somebody could claim it was theirs. Isla stared at it. It looked exactly like a loaf her own grandmother made, except this one had been sitting there since before most of the languages she knew even existed.

"That baker had no idea," Isla said softly. "He just put bread in the oven like it was a normal Tuesday."

She wandered along the wall and found more red paint — not art this time, but writing, blocky letters scratched or painted right onto the plaster. The same kind of political slogan she'd seen earlier, still legible, still shouting a dead man's name at a street that no longer existed. "People really did just write on walls here," she said, grinning despite everything. "Ancient graffiti. Some things never change."

A little further on, a brush uncovered a shape in the hardened ash that made Isla's breath catch — a hollow, a person-shaped space where the ash had closed tight around somebody and then the somebody had, over centuries, simply disappeared, leaving a mold behind like a footprint in snow. The archaeologist beside it worked slowly, respectfully, pouring in plaster to fill the hollow and keep its shape, the way you might press a key into wax just to remember its outline.

Isla didn't ask any more questions about that one. She just stood quietly for a moment, the way you do at a cemetery, and then let the stone pull her gently on.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Town Down the Coast
chapters.text:
The dust cleared on a different place entirely — a smaller town, right on the water, where the dig crews were pulling something astonishing out of the ground: an actual wooden door, hinges and all, still swinging slightly on rusted metal.

"Wood?" Isla said. "Real wood survived? From the same eruption?"

*Herculaneum,* the dust spelled out. *A smaller seaside town. Same volcano. Different kind of burial.* **Nearby Herculaneum was buried by the same eruption, but under a different kind of volcanic material that preserved things Pompeii couldn't** — actual wooden furniture, wooden beams, even rolled-up scrolls that had survived against every reasonable odd. Where Pompeii had been buried in falling ash and stone, Herculaneum had been covered by something that sealed in oxygen-starved pockets so tight that wood simply never rotted away.

Isla crouched by a wooden shelf still holding the ghost-shape of jars that had once sat on it. "So it's like two different detectives got two different kinds of evidence from the same crime scene," she said, delighted. "One town kept the paintings and the bread. The other kept the *furniture.*"

The stone hummed what she was fairly sure was agreement.

She followed a path back toward Pompeii's own dig site, where a crew had just uncovered a wall that made several people actually gasp. Isla pushed closer. Painted across the plaster, in colors still shockingly bright, were figures in a strange, dramatic scene — robed people, a winged figure, something that looked almost like a ceremony caught mid-breath.

"What is that?" Isla whispered.

*The Villa of the Mysteries,* the dust answered. *Nobody is fully sure what the painting shows.* **Archaeologists found colorful wall paintings, including the famous 'Villa of the Mysteries' paintings, showing some kind of mysterious ceremony that nobody has fully figured out even now.**

Isla's whole case-solving brain lit up like a struck match. "An actual unsolved mystery. A real one. That nobody's cracked in — however long it's been."

The stone hummed, almost like it was laughing at her. *Some mysteries,* it seemed to say, *stay mysteries. Even for very good detectives.*

"That," Isla said, grinning, "is the most annoying and also the best thing I've heard all day."
chapters.shout_line: A MYSTERY NOBODY'S CRACKED! FINALLY, A CHALLENGE!

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Town Nobody Remembered
chapters.text:
The dust shifted one final time, and Isla found herself standing beside men in old-fashioned coats, digging with shovels into a hillside, clearly not expecting much.

One of them struck something hard. He knelt, brushed dirt away with his sleeve, and froze.

"What year is this?" Isla asked the stone.

*1748,* it answered. **Pompeii had been mostly forgotten for centuries, until it was rediscovered in 1748, when workers digging in the area found ancient walls and artifacts** — pieces of the past that had simply been sitting there, waiting, the whole time, under hills that generations of people had farmed and walked over without ever knowing what lay beneath their boots.

Isla did some quick math and felt her jaw drop. "So this town sat buried for almost seventeen hundred years before anyone even realized it was here?" The stone hummed yes. "That's not a cold case," Isla said. "That's the coldest case in the entire history of cases."

The dust swirled faster now, years rushing past like a flipped calendar, and Isla watched careful brushes replace rough shovels, watched canvas tents and official signs appear, watched the dig site slowly turn into something she actually recognized from guidebooks: rope barriers, tour groups, a gift shop.

"**Pompeii's a real place people can actually visit now," she said, half to herself. "It's one of Italy's most-visited old sites — millions of people walk through it every single year," and somewhere behind her the stone hummed its agreement, as warm and steady as a nod.

She wandered the edge of the dig one last time and noticed something that made her stop cold: an entire section of the town still buried, untouched, weeds growing over a low grassy mound that the signs hadn't even labeled yet. "Wait — is that *not* dug up?"

*Only about two-thirds of Pompeii has been excavated so far,* the stone told her. *New things are still being found.* Isla stood very still, staring at the unopened ground, and felt something settle into place inside her chest — not the end of a mystery, but the realization that this particular case file would never actually close. There would always be more wall to brush clean, more fresco to uncover, more answer still waiting under the grass.

That, Isla decided, might be the best kind of mystery there was.

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Home, With Ash on the Carpet
chapters.text:
The dust rolled backward instead of forward this time, folding up like a photograph closing, and Isla blinked and found herself standing exactly where she'd started: her own bedroom, string-covered wall, the Pompeii photo pinned right where she'd left it.

The stone in her hand had gone cool and quiet again, ordinary gray, like nothing at all had happened.

Except — on the carpet by her sneaker sat one small fleck of pale gray ash, impossibly real, catching the lamplight like it had opinions about being there.

Isla picked it up carefully, the way you'd handle real evidence, and set it on her desk beside the stone. Two souvenirs now: one that had been a gift, and one she'd carried home herself, from a city that had spent seventeen hundred years keeping an entire afternoon exactly the way it was.

She looked at her corkboard, at the red string, at the card that said **POMPEII**, and for once she didn't cross it off her mystery wall. She just added a new line underneath it in careful handwriting: *Case not closed. Two-thirds still buried. Keep watching.*

Her teacher had assigned an evacuation-map project for the week — streets, exits, a way out in case of emergency, due Friday. Isla had been dreading it as busywork. Now she climbed into bed thinking about stepping stones built to solve two problems at once, about a young man who wrote down exactly what he saw because somebody, someday, might need to know, and about a mountain that was still out there right now, still being watched, still worth taking seriously.

Tomorrow, she had a map of her own to draw, and for the first time all week, she actually knew exactly why it mattered.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow, she had a map of her own to draw, and for the first time all week, she actually knew exactly why it mattered.

story.title: Priya, Dev, and the Spray-Gate Rainbow
story.subtitle: A squirt, a sunbeam, and a trip inside a raindrop

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Backyard Rainbow
chapters.text:
Priya was drawing a rainbow on the living room rug. "Red, orange, yellow," she mumbled, picking her crayons.

"Boring, boring, same old stripes," said Dev. He aimed his water pistol at her page, just for fun.

SPLOOSH! A fine mist floated up into a sunbeam from the window.

A tiny rainbow popped up inside the mist. Then it started to glow, bright as a nightlight.

"Whoa," said Priya. "Rainbows don't usually do that."

The glowing mist swirled into a ring, big enough to step through. A small light, shaped like a droplet, blinked inside it.

"I'm Ray," it said. "Want to see how I'm made? You need the **sun behind you**" — it pointed at the window — "and rain, or spray, in front."

Dev looked down at his water pistol. "I did that!"

"You did," said Ray. "Now hold hands and step in."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Inside the Raindrop
chapters.text:
They landed inside something round and squishy, like a giant glass marble. Light dripped down the walls.

"Welcome to a raindrop," said Ray. "This is where the magic starts."

A beam of sunlight zoomed in through one side.

"Watch it bend," said Ray. "Light slows down going from air into water, so it turns, like a car turning a corner. That bending is called **refraction**."

Priya traced the beam's path with her finger. "It bounces off the back, too!"

"Exactly," said Ray. "It hits the back wall, bounces like a ball off a wall, and bends again on its way out."

Dev squirted a tiny spray right at the beam, just to watch it wiggle.

"IT BENDS!" he shouted.

"Easy there, sharpshooter," laughed Priya, flicking water droplets off her sleeve.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Roy G. Biv
chapters.text:
The beam of light stretched out like taffy and split into a row of colors.

"Whoa," said Priya. "Sunlight looks white outside, but it's really all these colors mixed together."

"Smart kid," said Ray. "Each color bends by a slightly different amount. That's how the drop sorts them out."

Dev counted on his fingers. "Red, orange, yellow, green, blue... I ran out of fingers."

"There's indigo and violet too," said Ray. "Some people say **Roy G. Biv** to remember the order."

"Roy G. Biv," Priya repeated, giggling. "Sounds like my uncle."

"Here's a clue," said Ray. "**Red** bends the least, so it ends up on the outside edge. **Violet** bends the most, so it's on the inside."

Priya pointed, outside to inside. "Red... orange... yellow... all the way to violet!"

"Got it in one," said Ray.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Man with the Water Bowl
chapters.text:
Ray waved a hand, and the raindrop walls melted into a sunny rooftop, long, long ago.

A man sat with a bowl of water, watching light dance across it.

"This is **Ibn al-Haytham**," said Ray. "About a thousand years ago, he studied how light travels and how our eyes see it."

"Did he figure out rainbows?" asked Dev.

"He got the ball rolling," said Ray. "Other thinkers used his ideas later."

Priya watched the man scribble notes. "He's basically doing homework."

"The best kind," said Ray. "The kind with water and sunbeams."

Dev squirted his water pistol at a sunny patch on the rooftop, and a tiny rainbow flickered in the mist.

"I'm doing his homework too!" Dev announced.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Glass Ball
chapters.text:
The rooftop shimmered, and they stood beside a man holding a big glass ball filled with water.

"This is **Kamal al-Din al-Farisi**," said Ray. "In **1304**, he used glass balls like this one to copy a raindrop."

He held the ball up to the sun, and colors spilled across the wall.

"He's making a rainbow on purpose!" said Priya.

"That's the idea," said Ray. "Testing the ball helped him work out how a real raindrop bends and splits light."

Dev pressed his nose close to the glass. "Can I try?"

The man smiled and let Dev hold the ball toward the sun. A stripe of color landed right on Dev's sneaker.

"I made a shoe rainbow," Dev announced, delighted.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Newton's Triangle
chapters.text:
Next, Ray led them into a cozy room with candles and a glass triangle on the table.

"This is **Isaac Newton's** room," said Ray. "In **1666**, he held a glass **prism**, shaped like that triangle, up to a sunbeam."

Priya picked up the prism and turned it slowly. A fan of rainbow colors spread across the wall.

"The prism splits the light, just like the raindrop did!" she said.

"Newton proved that plain white sunlight has all those colors hiding inside it," said Ray.

Dev tried to catch the colors with his hands. "They're not sticky. They just float there."

"That's light for you," said Ray. "Pretty, but impossible to hold."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Secret Bottom Half
chapters.text:
Outside the window, a real rainbow arched over a meadow.

"Why is it only a curve, not a full circle?" asked Priya.

"Good question," said Ray. "A rainbow is really a **full circle**. The ground just blocks the bottom half, so we only see the top arc."

Dev gasped. "So there's a secret bottom half?"

"Hiding underground, sort of," said Ray. "But people flying in **airplanes** sometimes see the whole circle, because there's no ground in the way up there."

Priya imagined looking down at a rainbow donut from a plane window. "I want a window seat."

"Me too," said Dev, "so I can squirt it."

"You cannot squirt a rainbow from an airplane," said Priya, rolling her eyes — but she was laughing.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Your Very Own Rainbow
chapters.text:
Back in the meadow, Priya noticed something odd. "Dev, can you see the same rainbow I see?"

Dev squinted. "I guess so?"

"Actually, no," said Ray. "Everyone sees their **own personal rainbow**, made from different raindrops, because of exactly where their eyes are standing."

"So I have a Priya rainbow and you have a Dev rainbow?" asked Priya.

"Exactly," said Ray. "Nobody else in the whole world sees your exact one."

Just then, a **second rainbow** appeared above the first, fainter, with its colors flipped upside down.

"DOUBLE RAINBOW!" shouted Dev.

"That happens when light bounces twice inside some of the drops," said Ray. "It flips the color order the second time."

Priya studied both arcs. "Red's on the bottom of this one and on top of that one. Neat."

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: No Pot of Gold Required
chapters.text:
As the sun dipped low, Ray floated closer. "One more trick. At night, moonlight can make a rainbow too. It's called a **moonbow**."

"Is it rainbow-colored?" asked Dev.

"Mostly it looks silvery white to our eyes," said Ray, "though a camera can catch the hidden colors."

Priya tilted her head. "People used to think rainbows were magic, right?"

"All sorts of stories," said Ray. "Some say a rainbow is a bridge called **Bifrost**, connecting Earth to the home of the gods. Others tell of a rainbow after a great flood, as a sign of a promise to a man named Noah."

"And a **pot of gold** at the end?" asked Dev, eyes wide.

"That one's probably just a fun legend," said Ray gently, "because a rainbow moves whenever you move. You can **never actually touch** one."

"No pot of gold," sighed Dev. "But I've got my water pistol."

"Exactly what you need," said Ray. "A rainbow needs both sunshine and water drops in the air at the very same time. That's why they show up after rain, when the sun peeks back out. Scientists who study how light bends and bounces call it the science of **optics**."

The mist around them began to shrink, pulling them gently backward.

Priya and Dev tumbled onto the living room rug, sketchbook and water pistol right where they'd left them.

Priya looked at her drawing, then added one more thing: a tiny glowing droplet, waving, beside her rainbow.

"Goodnight, Ray," she whispered.

story.ending_line: Sweet dreams, Priya. Sweet dreams, Dev. Keep looking up.

true_facts.text: To see a rainbow, you need the **sun behind you** and rain or spray in front of you.
Sunlight goes into a raindrop, bends, bounces off the back wall, and bends again on its way out.
That bending is called **refraction** — light turns because it slows down going from air into water.
Sunlight looks white, but it's really **all the colors mixed together**.
The color order in a rainbow is **red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, and violet** — Roy G. Biv.
**Red** always sits on the outside edge of a rainbow, and **violet** sits on the inside.
In **1666**, Isaac Newton used a glass **prism** to split sunlight into the same rainbow of colors.
A rainbow is really a **full circle**, but the ground blocks the bottom half so we only see an arc.
From an **airplane**, people sometimes see the whole circle rainbow, with no ground in the way.
Everyone sees their **own personal rainbow**, made from different raindrops, because of exactly where they're standing.
Sometimes a fainter **second rainbow** appears above the first, with its colors flipped.
The story of a **pot of gold** at a rainbow's end is just a fun legend — a rainbow moves whenever you do.
Because of that, you can **never actually touch** a rainbow.
Scientists who study how light bends and bounces call it the science of **optics**.

facts.text: A rainbow forms when sunlight enters a raindrop, bends, reflects off the inside back of the drop, and bends again as it exits.
This bending of light is called refraction, and it happens because light slows down and changes direction when it moves from air into water.
White sunlight is actually made of many colors mixed together, and raindrops separate them because each color bends by a slightly different amount.
The classic rainbow color order is red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, and violet, often remembered with the name 'Roy G. Biv'.
Red always appears on the outer edge of a rainbow and violet on the inner edge because red bends the least and violet bends the most.
To see a rainbow, the sun must be behind you and rain (or spray) must be in front of you.
Rainbows are actually full circles, but we usually only see an arc because the ground blocks the bottom half.
From an airplane, people sometimes see a complete circular rainbow because there is no ground in the way.
Every person actually sees a slightly different rainbow, made from different raindrops, because the angle of light to your eyes is unique to your position.
A rainbow always appears in the part of the sky directly opposite the sun, centered on a point called the antisolar point.
Sometimes a fainter second rainbow appears above the main one, with its colors reversed, caused by light bouncing twice inside the raindrops.
The dark strip of sky between a primary and secondary rainbow is called Alexander's band, named after the ancient Greek philosopher Alexander of Aphrodisias who described it around 200 AD.
Rainbows can also form in mist, waterfalls, garden hose spray, and even moonlight, where they are called moonbows.
Moonbows are usually so faint that they look white or gray to human eyes, though cameras can capture their colors.
The scientist Isaac Newton showed in the 1660s that a glass prism could split white light into the same rainbow of colors, proving light itself contains all the colors.
The Persian scientist Ibn al-Haytham and later Kamal al-Din al-Farisi studied light and rainbows in raindrops centuries before Newton, around the 1000s and 1300s.
Many cultures have myths about rainbows, such as the Norse story of Bifrost, a rainbow bridge connecting Earth to the home of the gods.
In the Bible, the rainbow appears as a sign of a promise from God to Noah after a great flood.
Many cultures tell of a pot of gold at the end of a rainbow, especially in Irish folklore involving leprechauns, though a rainbow's end is never a real fixed spot since it moves as you move.
Because a rainbow depends on where the viewer stands, you can never actually walk up to or touch one.
Rainbows need both sunlight and water droplets at the same time, which is why they often appear during or right after a rain shower when the sun peeks out.
A rainbow's size in the sky is always about the same, spanning roughly 42 degrees from the antisolar point for the primary bow.
The rainbow flag, created by artist Gilbert Baker in 1978, uses rainbow colors as a symbol of pride and diversity.
Rainbows are studied in a branch of science called optics, which explores how light behaves, bends, and reflects.
