story.title: Jack, Ellie, and the Shark Tooth That Glowed
story.subtitle: A dive through four hundred million years of fins, teeth, and one very leathery purse.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Tooth Under the Bed
chapters.text:
Jack had built an ocean cave out of couch cushions. Ellie's mermaid doll sat on top, tail sparkling under the lamp. "Mermaids don't live in cushion caves," Jack said. Ellie stuck out her tongue. "Mine does."

While hunting for a lost sock, Jack's hand hit something hard under the bed. He pulled out an old necklace. A gray, pointed tooth hung from the string, bigger than his thumb.

"That's not a dog tooth," Jack said, turning it over. "I bet it's a shark tooth."

Ellie poked it. The tooth glowed, blue-green, like a nightlight waking up.

"Did you SEE that?!" Ellie shrieked.

Jack grabbed the tooth with both hands. The glow spread across the floor like water pouring from nowhere. **WHOOSH!** The bedroom melted into blue.

They landed in warm water, sunlight dancing far above. Long, sleek shapes slid past, built like no fish either of them had ever drawn.

A woman in an old diving suit swam up, smiling behind her mask. "Welcome," she said. "You found my tooth. I'm Dr. Clark."

"Are those sharks?" Jack asked, pointing.

"The very first kind," said Dr. Clark. "Sharks have swum in oceans for more than **400 million years** — since before there were dinosaurs, or even trees."

Ellie's jaw dropped. "Older than TREES?"

"Much older," said Dr. Clark. "And their skeleton isn't hard bone like yours. It's soft and bendy, like the squishy part inside your ear. That's called cartilage."

Jack squeezed his own ear. "Whoa. Bendy bones."

"Let's go see more," said Dr. Clark, and the water pulled them gently forward.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Tooth as Big as a Hand
chapters.text:
The water grew cooler and darker. Something huge drifted far off, bigger than any shark they had seen yet.

Jack squinted. "Is that shadow... a whale?"

"That was **Megalodon**," said Dr. Clark. "The biggest shark that ever lived. But don't worry — Megalodon is extinct now. That means every single one is gone, and has been for a very long time."

Ellie breathed out. "Gone gone?"

"Gone gone," said Dr. Clark gently. "But we still know about it, thanks to something it left behind."

A huge triangle tooth drifted down and landed in the sand, as long as Jack's whole hand.

Jack picked it up, eyes wide. "THIS is a tooth?!"

"A fossil tooth," said Dr. Clark. "Fossils are things from long ago that turned hard as rock. A shark's bendy skeleton is too soft to leave much behind, so teeth are almost all we have left to study."

"So this tooth is like... a clue," Jack said.

"Exactly like a clue," said Dr. Clark, nodding.

Ellie held the tooth against her own small hand. It covered her whole palm.

"I would NOT want this shark near my mermaid," she said.

Jack laughed so hard he nearly dropped the tooth. "Good thing it's gone, then. Your mermaid is safe."

Ellie tucked the thought away, satisfied, and they swam on into brighter water.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: More Teeth Than You Can Count
chapters.text:
A sleek shark glided past, rows and rows of white triangles inside its open mouth.

Ellie gasped. "That's a LOT of teeth."

"That's a **great white shark**," said Dr. Clark. "It can grow up to about **20 feet long**, and those teeth have tiny jagged edges, like a steak knife, for catching seals and fish."

Jack counted rows with his finger, swimming closer but not too close. "One, two, three... there's MORE teeth hiding behind the front ones!"

"Good eye," said Dr. Clark. "Sharks don't just have one set of teeth like you do. They grow new ones their whole life. When a tooth falls out, another moves forward to take its place."

"So they never run out?" Jack asked.

"Never," said Dr. Clark. "A shark can lose and grow thousands of teeth in a lifetime."

Ellie wiggled her own loose front tooth. "I only get ONE new tooth. That's so unfair."

"Guess you'll just have fewer visits from the tooth fairy than a shark would," Jack said.

Ellie swatted at him, giggling, and a cloud of sand puffed up where her hand hit the seafloor. Jack swam backward, laughing, pretending to be chased by the cloud.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Sandpaper Skin and the Fastest Fin
chapters.text:
Dr. Clark let a passing shark brush close to her glove. "Touch its side," she said. "Gently."

Jack ran one finger along the shark's skin. He yelped. "It's SCRATCHY! Like sandpaper!"

"That's exactly what it is," said Dr. Clark. "Shark skin is covered in thousands of tiny points called denticles. They make the skin rough, but they also help the shark slide through water smoothly, with less drag."

"Drag?" Ellie asked.

"Drag is water pushing back, slowing something down," said Dr. Clark. "Less drag means more speed."

Right on cue, a streak of silver shot past so fast the water rippled.

"WHOA! What was THAT?!" Jack shouted.

"That was a shortfin mako," said Dr. Clark. "The fastest shark in the ocean. It uses quick bursts of speed to catch fast fish like tuna before they even know it's coming."

Ellie tried to swim after it and only managed a wobbly doggy paddle. "No fair. It's cheating."

"It's not cheating," Jack said, grinning. "It's just got better skin than you."

Ellie flicked water at him. Jack flicked it right back, and Dr. Clark laughed so hard bubbles shot out of her mask.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Secret Radar
chapters.text:
A strange shark swam into view, its head stretched wide and flat, like someone had squashed it sideways.

Ellie blinked. "Why is its head like THAT?"

"That's a **hammerhead shark**," said Dr. Clark. "Its eyes sit far apart on that wide head, giving it an almost all-the-way-around view, perfect for spotting prey hiding in the sand."

Jack swam a little closer, careful not to get too near. Tiny dots covered the shark's snout. "What are those little dots?"

"Good find," said Dr. Clark. "Those are jelly-filled dots that feel tiny electric signals, the kind every living thing gives off just by moving its muscles. That's how a shark finds a fish hiding under the sand, even with its eyes shut."

"So it's got its own secret radar," Jack said.

"Close enough," said Dr. Clark, smiling.

Ellie hid her mermaid doll behind her back, just in case. "Can it feel ME?"

"Only in the water," said Dr. Clark. "And it's much more interested in finding dinner than finding mermaids."

Ellie peeked the doll back out, satisfied. The hammerhead swam on, swinging its wide head side to side, like it was checking both ways before crossing an underwater street.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Gentle Giant
chapters.text:
The water grew suddenly bright, and a shadow the size of a school bus slid overhead.

Jack froze. "Is that... is that going to EAT us?"

"Don't worry," said Dr. Clark, laughing. "That's a **whale shark**, the biggest fish in the whole world, over **40 feet long**. It only eats tiny floating food called plankton, by swimming along with its giant mouth open like a scoop."

Ellie relaxed. "So it's gentle?"

"Very gentle," said Dr. Clark. "Some whale sharks live to be **100 years old** or even older, one of the longest lives of any fish."

Jack watched it glide by, slow and enormous. "A hundred years. That's older than my grandpa."

Down near the coral, something small flopped from rock to rock, using its fins like little paddles.

"Is that shark... WALKING?" Ellie squealed.

"That's an epaulette shark," said Dr. Clark. "It can scoot across the reef on its fins, and it can go hours with barely any air in the water around it. Handy, since tide pools sometimes dry up."

Jack tried to copy the walk with his arms, flopping sideways through the water. Ellie laughed so hard bubbles shot out of her nose.

"You look more like a flipping pancake," she giggled.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Mermaid's Purse
chapters.text:
Something leathery and dark drifted past, shaped like a little pouch with curly strings at each corner.

Ellie caught it gently in her hands. "What IS this? It's so weird."

"That's a shark egg case," said Dr. Clark. "Some sharks lay their eggs inside a case like that one, instead of having live babies. Divers nicknamed them 'mermaid's purses.'"

Ellie's whole face lit up. "A real mermaid's purse?! I'm keeping this forever."

"You can't keep the real one," Jack teased, "but I bet you can draw it."

Dr. Clark gathered them close as more sharks circled, slow and calm, further out. "Sharks sit at the top of the ocean's food chain," she said. "That means they help keep every other animal's numbers balanced, so the whole ocean stays healthy."

"Like a referee," Jack said.

"Exactly like a referee," said Dr. Clark. "And here's something worth knowing: sharks hurting people is very rare. It's actually people who hurt far more sharks, every single year."

Ellie frowned. "That doesn't seem fair to the sharks."

"It isn't," said Dr. Clark. "That's why so many people now work hard to protect them."

"Is that why you studied sharks?" Jack asked.

Dr. Clark smiled. "I'm Eugenie Clark. People called me the Shark Lady. I spent years studying sharks and proved they're curious. Some can even be trained, like a dog learning a trick."

Jack grinned. "Best job ever."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Back on the Carpet
chapters.text:
The glow folded back in on itself, blue turning gold, gold turning into bedroom light.

Jack and Ellie landed with a soft thump on the carpet, right back inside their cushion ocean cave.

The tooth necklace lay quiet in Jack's hand, not glowing anymore, just an ordinary gray tooth on a string.

Ellie looked down and found something new beside her mermaid doll: a small leathery pouch, curly strings and all, resting on the carpet like it had followed her home.

"Is that...?" Jack started.

"My mermaid's purse," Ellie said happily, scooping it up. "Dr. Clark must have let me keep a little one."

Jack turned the tooth over in his fingers one more time. "Four hundred million years," he mumbled. "That's wild."

"Older than trees," Ellie reminded him, grinning.

"Older than trees," Jack agreed.

He tucked the necklace under his pillow. Ellie tucked her mermaid's purse right beside it.

"Goodnight, Jack," Ellie yawned. "Don't let a megalodon nibble your toes."

"Goodnight, Ellie," Jack said. "Don't let a mermaid steal your blanket."

Jack flopped back onto the cushions, the cave quiet now, the whole ocean folded up and waiting for tomorrow night.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Jack. Goodnight, Ellie. Dive well, and dream deep.

facts.text: Sharks are fish whose skeletons are made of flexible cartilage instead of hard bone, like the stretchy material in human ears.

Sharks grow and lose thousands of teeth over a lifetime, with new teeth constantly moving forward to replace worn or lost ones.

Bull sharks tolerate both salty ocean water and fresh river water, and have been found swimming far upriver.
Nurse sharks can pump water over their gills while resting on the sea floor, so they do not have to keep swimming to breathe.

story.title: Leo and the Sleepy Train
story.subtitle: A nighttime ride through why everybody sleeps, with Hoot the owl

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Glowing Owl
chapters.text:
Leo circled his wooden trains on the rug. One more lap, he thought.

The window went dark. The corner by the closet looked extra shadowy tonight.

Leo scooted closer to his lamp.

Then his owl nightlight ruffled its feathers. Its round eyes glowed bright gold.

"Psst, Leo," said the owl. "Want to find out why everyone sleeps? Even owls. Even you."

Leo's train tracks began to hum. CHUFF. CHUFF. The little train grew big enough to climb into.

"I'm Hoot," said the owl, hopping onto the front car. "Hold on tight."

The train rolled right through the wall, into a glowing room from long ago.

A boy slept on a cot. His eyelids twitched, flick-flick-flick.

Leo leaned close. "His eyes are moving! Under his eyelids!"

"Good eyes, Leo," said Hoot. "Two scientists, Eugene and Nathaniel, saw that exact thing in **1953**. They named it REM sleep — eyes that move while you dream."

Leo grinned. "I found it first!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Loop-the-Loop Track
chapters.text:
The train climbed a looping track, round and round.

"Why do we keep going in circles?" Leo asked, dizzy.

"Because sleep goes in circles too," said Hoot. "Every **90 minutes**, your brain takes a loop. Quiet sleep, then dream sleep. Round and round, all night."

Leo counted the loops on his fingers. "One loop, two loops, three loops!"

"Keep counting," said Hoot. "Each loop helps your body rest."

The train dipped low, then rose high, like a gentle wave.

Leo giggled. "It's like a lullaby ride!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Dream Depot
chapters.text:
The train stopped at a station glowing purple, full of floating dream-pictures.

"This is dream sleep," said Hoot. "Your brain gets busy, almost like when you're awake."

Leo reached for his arm. It flopped like a noodle. "Whoa! My arm is wiggly!"

"That's right," said Hoot. "During dream sleep your muscles go soft and floppy. Your body can't act out your dreams, like running or flying."

Leo tried to lift his noodle arm and laughed when it flopped back down.

"No flying tonight, Leo," hooted Hoot, laughing too.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Memory Library
chapters.text:
Next stop: shelves and shelves of glowing boxes, each one a memory.

"What's in here?" Leo asked, tapping a box labeled TRAIN TRACKS.

"Your brain sorts today's memories while you sleep," said Hoot. "Like the new track you built this morning."

Leo remembered his tricky curve of track. "I finally got that curve to fit!"

"Sleep helps you keep that trick," said Hoot. "Tomorrow you'll remember it even better."

Leo patted the glowing box gently, like tucking in a friend.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Baby Owl Nest
chapters.text:
A soft hoo-hoo came from a mossy nest. Inside, a baby owl slept, eyes shut tight.

"Newborn babies sleep a LOT," whispered Hoot. "About **14 to 17 hours** a day, in little naps."

Leo whispered back, "That's way more naps than me!"

"Growing takes lots of rest," said Hoot.

The baby owl stirred, yawned a tiny yawn, and settled again.

Leo tiptoed away so he wouldn't wake her. "Shh. Sleep well, little owl."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: One Eye Open
chapters.text:
The train rolled along a moonlit shore. Dolphins leaped, then floated, one eye open, one eye closed.

"Why's that eye still open?" Leo asked.

"Dolphins sleep with half their brain at a time," said Hoot. "One eye watches for trouble while the other half rests."

Leo tried it, squinting one eye and leaving the other open. He wobbled and laughed. "Hard!"

"Good thing you've got two closing eyes," said Hoot, nudging him gently.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Giraffes and Bats
chapters.text:
The train huffed up a hill. A giraffe stood munching leaves, barely swaying.

"Giraffes barely sleep," said Hoot. "Sometimes under **two hours** a day, in little standing naps."

Leo pointed at a cave nearby, full of upside-down bats. "What about them?"

"Some bats sleep up to **20 hours** a day," said Hoot. "Champion sleepers!"

Leo shook his head. "Two hours, twenty hours — everyone sleeps different amounts!"

"Just right for them," said Hoot. "Just right for you too."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Back to the Rug
chapters.text:
The train looped one last time, then shrank small again, right back on Leo's rug.

"So... why do we sleep?" Leo asked.

"To grow, to remember, to rest your busy brain," said Hoot. "You sleep almost **a third** of your whole life. That's a lot of important rest."

Leo looked at the shadowy corner. It didn't seem so scary now. Just a cozy spot where owls and trains both get their rest.

He climbed into bed, the owl nightlight glowing softly beside him.

"Night, Hoot," Leo whispered.

"Night, Leo," said Hoot. "Dream bright, sleep tight."

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Leo. Dream bright, sleep tight.

fact_pack.summary: Every person and almost every animal sleeps, though scientists still study exactly why. Sleep runs in repeating brain cycles that help the body grow, heal, and sort memories.

facts.text: In 1953, Eugene Aserinsky and Nathaniel Kleitman at the University of Chicago discovered rapid eye movement (REM) sleep by watching a sleeping boy's eyes twitch under his eyelids.
A night's sleep is made of repeating cycles about 90 minutes long, moving between quiet non-REM sleep and active, dream-filled REM sleep.
During REM sleep the brain is almost as busy as when awake, but the body's muscles go limp so the sleeper cannot act out dreams.
The deepest non-REM stage triggers the most growth hormone release, one reason growing children need extra sleep.
A tiny brain region called the suprachiasmatic nucleus, just above where the eye nerves cross, works as the body's master clock for sleeping and waking.
'Circadian,' the body's roughly 24-hour clock, comes from Latin words meaning 'about a day.'
In 2017 the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine went to Jeffrey Hall, Michael Rosbash, and Michael Young for finding the genes that keep the circadian clock ticking.
The sleepy-time hormone melatonin was first isolated in 1958 by scientist Aaron Lerner's team, extracted from animal pineal glands.
Sleep helps the brain sort the day's experiences into long-term memories, so good sleep can help someone remember what they practiced or learned.
A nightly 'rinse cycle' called the glymphatic system flushes waste out of the sleeping brain.

story.title: Arjun and the Umpire of Ninety Minutes
story.subtitle: A comic-book journey through why we sleep.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Panel That Blinked
chapters.text:
Arjun lay flat under his blanket, torch clamped in his teeth, reading the last page of *Captain Boundary* issue fourteen.

"Lights out," called his mum from the hallway.

"Five more minutes," Arjun called back, same as always.

He never got five more minutes. Tonight, though, something strange happened instead.

The comic's last panel — a close-up of Captain Boundary's eyes — started to twitch. Little lines zipped back and forth across the page, like someone had drawn speed marks over his eyeballs. Arjun poked the paper. The eyes blinked at him.

**BZZZT.** The page lit up white, and out stepped a cartoon owl in a long coat, one wing raised like he was giving a decision at the crease.

"NOT OUT," said the owl. "Not yet, anyway. I'm Umpire Hoot. I call sleep the way you call cricket — and tonight you're on strike."

"Why were the eyes doing that twitchy thing?" Arjun asked.

"Good eye." Hoot tapped the panel. "In **1953**, two scientists named **Eugene Aserinsky** and **Nathaniel Kleitman**, at the University of Chicago, watched a sleeping boy's eyelids and saw them flicker like that, fast, side to side. Nobody had studied it properly before. They named it **REM sleep** — the eyes move Rapidly while the rest of the sleeper lies still."

"Like speed lines," said Arjun. "In a comic, when something's moving fast, you draw lines."

Hoot's beak dropped open. "That is exactly what REM looks like under the eyelid. Nobody's put it that well before. Shall we go see the rest of the innings?"

He tapped the panel twice. The page folded open like a door.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Ninety-Minute Innings
chapters.text:
They stepped through into somewhere that was half cricket pitch, half science lab — a cot sat where the batting crease should be, with wires taped gently to a snoozing boy's forehead.

"Each night isn't one long sleep," Hoot said. "It's cycles, about **90 minutes** each, flipping between calm, quiet sleep and busy, dream-filled REM sleep, back and forth, all night."

Arjun did the math out loud, the way he counted overs. "If you sleep for eight hours... that's... five cycles?"

"Just about," said Hoot. "Close enough to call it right."

The boy on the cot twitched his fingers mid-dream, like he was trying to swing a bat. Nothing happened.

"He's dreaming he's batting," Arjun said. "Why isn't he actually swinging?"

"Because during REM, the brain's almost as busy as when you're awake," said Hoot, "but the body's muscles go soft and still, like a controller unplugged. That's so sleepers don't act out whatever wild thing they're dreaming."

Arjun grinned. "So it's the ultimate no-ball. Everything's happening and nothing's happening."

"Best description I've heard all century," said Hoot. "Next over."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Growth Hormone Power-Up
chapters.text:
A glowing bar hovered over the sleeping boy's head now, climbing like a scoreboard.

"What's that?" Arjun asked.

"Growth hormone," said Hoot. "A chemical signal that tells the body to grow and repair itself. It gets released most during the deepest part of quiet sleep — one reason growing kids need plenty of it."

Arjun watched the bar spike and dip, over and over, matching the cycles Hoot had shown him. "So sleep's basically training," he said. "You level up while you're not even trying."

"You level up precisely because you're not trying," said Hoot. "That's the trick of it."

Arjun thought about his coach, who always said the same two things after practice: stretch, and go to bed on time. He'd always figured the second one was just a coach being a coach.

"Turns out," Arjun muttered, "he wasn't bluffing."

He pictured his own scoreboard bar climbing while he slept, then imagined explaining that to his team. "Sleep nets," he said. "That's what we should call practice." Hoot nearly fell off his branch laughing.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Body's Umpire
chapters.text:
A soft ticking filled the air, like a stump mic picking up a watch.

"That's the body's umpire," said Hoot, pointing to a tiny glowing nest of cells, tucked right where two nerves from the eyes crossed. "Scientists call it the **suprachiasmatic nucleus** — a mouthful, so most people just call it the master clock. It decides when you feel sleepy and when you feel awake, on its own schedule."

"Like it's giving out decisions all day," said Arjun. "Sleepy... not sleepy... sleepy..."

"Precisely. And that schedule has a name too: **circadian**. Have a guess."

Arjun turned the word over. "Circa... that sounds like 'around.' And -dian... day?"

Hoot's feathers puffed up with pride. "Bang on. It comes from old words meaning 'about a day' — because the clock runs on a cycle close to 24 hours, give or take."

"So my body's got its own umpire, running its own matches, every single day."

"Every single day," Hoot agreed. "Whether you ask for five more minutes or not."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Trophy Case
chapters.text:
They passed a glass case lit up like a man-of-the-match display, three medals inside.

"In **2017**, the Nobel Prize — science's biggest award for discoveries — went to three scientists: **Jeffrey Hall**, **Michael Rosbash**, and **Michael Young**. They had found the actual genes, tiny instructions inside the body's cells, that keep the circadian clock ticking."

Arjun squinted at the medal labels, completely out of order, and rearranged them alphabetically without being asked. "There," he said. "Hall, Rosbash, Young. Much tidier."

"Scientists rarely sort themselves that neatly," said Hoot, "but I appreciate the effort."

"So the clock isn't just a feeling," Arjun said. "It's actually built into us. In our cells."

"Built in," Hoot agreed, "same as yours seems built to want five more minutes."

Arjun laughed. "That's not a gene. That's just me."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Melatonin Ink
chapters.text:
On a desk shaped suspiciously like Arjun's own, a bottle of ink sat glowing, brightening and dimming like it was breathing.

"That's melatonin," said Hoot. "The body's sleepy-time chemical. A scientist named **Aaron Lerner** and his team first studied it properly in **1958**, pulling it from a tiny gland deep in the brain."

"Why's it doing the glowy breathing thing?"

"Melatonin rises when it gets dark," said Hoot, "and dims back down when light returns. It's one of the signals telling your body which way the match is heading — toward sleep, or toward waking up."

Arjun cupped his hands over Hoot's torch, blocking the light. The ink bottle brightened at once.

"Told you," said Hoot. "Dark in, melatonin up."

"So night-lights are basically cheating the umpire," said Arjun.

"A little," Hoot admitted. "Everyone does it sometimes."

Arjun uncupped his hands, and the glow dimmed back down, patient as ever.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Night Shift
chapters.text:
The next page burst open into a two-page spread: half ocean, half grassy plain.

A dolphin cruised past with one eye open, watching them.

"Dolphins — and some seals — sleep with only half their brain resting at a time," said Hoot. "One side naps while the other stays alert, one eye open, so they can still watch for danger or keep swimming."

"That's basically keeping a fielder on the boundary while the rest of the team naps," said Arjun.

"An excellent comparison," said Hoot.

Across the grass, a giraffe stood very still, eyes half shut, then snapped fully awake a few seconds later.

"Giraffes are some of the shortest sleepers of any large animal," said Hoot. "Sometimes under two hours a day, taken in quick naps while standing up."

Arjun stared. "Two hours? I can't even finish a comic in two hours."

"Different bodies, different rules," said Hoot. "Nobody's wrong. Just different innings."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Scrapbook Rinse
chapters.text:
A pile of loose comic panels lay scattered across the floor, exactly like the mess under Arjun's bed.

"Sleep helps sort all this," said Hoot, waving a wing at the mess. "The brain uses sleep to file the day's moments into long-term memory — the stuff you'll actually remember later, like a new batting trick you practiced."

Arjun started stacking panels into piles without thinking — keepers in one stack, scraps in another. "So sleeping is like cleaning my room, except it's cleaning my head."

"Better," said Hoot. "There's also a nightly rinse called the **glymphatic system** — think of it as a washing machine for the brain, flushing out the gunk that builds up during the day."

"My brain has a washing machine." Arjun looked delighted. "Does it have a spin cycle?"

"Every single night," said Hoot. "Whether you ask for it or not."

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Randy's Wide-Awake Record
chapters.text:
A dusty old noticeboard appeared next, pinned with a yellowed newspaper clipping.

"In **1964**, a seventeen-year-old named **Randy Gardner**, from San Diego, stayed awake for about **eleven days** straight — for a school science project," said Hoot. "One of the longest stretches without sleep anyone's ever properly recorded."

Arjun's eyes went wide. "Eleven days? I can barely survive without my five more minutes."

"Here's the thing," said Hoot, suddenly serious. "Doctors don't recommend anyone try to beat that, or copy it at all. Going without sleep, even for a short while, quickly messes with your mood, your attention, your memory — everything gets worse, fast."

Arjun thought about it. "So it's a cool story. Not a cool plan."

"Exactly that," said Hoot, looking relieved. "Best way I've heard it put."

"Then I vote," said Arjun, "for sleep. Actual sleep. Tonight."

The noticeboard folded itself away. The comic page reappeared under Arjun's torch, Captain Boundary's eyes finally still, closed on the final panel.

"Last call," said Hoot, already fading back into the ink. "Lights out?"

Arjun clicked off his torch without being asked. "Lights out," he agreed.

In the morning, tucked in the spine of issue fourteen, there was a single new panel that hadn't been there before: a small cartoon owl in an umpire's coat, one wing raised.

**NOT OUT**, it said. **Just resting.**

story.ending_line: Tomorrow there was a cricket match to win, and for once, Arjun meant to be wide awake for all of it.

story.title: Noah and the Ninety-Minute Loop
story.subtitle: A late-night tour through the science of sleep, guided by something that lives in a dead phone screen.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: Loading...
chapters.text:
Noah was two attempts into a boss fight at 12:47 a.m., headset on, blue light washing over his face, when his phone screen died mid-combo. Not off — dead green, like an old computer terminal nobody makes anymore.

Text crawled across it, pixel by pixel: SYSTEM IDLE TOO LONG. INITIATE SLEEP.EXE?

He laughed. "Funny firmware." He tapped NO.

The screen folded open anyway, hinge-style, and something stepped out of it: a low, fox-shaped shimmer made of scanlines, ears like antenna bars.

"Took you long enough," it said. "I'm Circa. Your clock."

"My clock doesn't talk."

"Your clock has been trying to talk to you since roughly 2013 a.m., which doesn't exist, which is the point."

Noah set down the controller, mostly because the fox was standing on his keyboard. "What do you want?"

"To show you what you skip every night. In **1953**, two researchers named **Eugene Aserinsky and Nathaniel Kleitman** were watching a sleeping kid's eyelids twitch, fast, back and forth — and that's how they found REM sleep, the stage where you dream." Circa's tail flicked like a loading bar. "Kleitman spent his whole career on this. People still call him the father of the field."

"The father of naps."

"Press the button and find out," said Circa, nodding at a new glowing prompt: CONTINUE?

Noah pressed it.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Ninety-Minute Loop
chapters.text:
The floor dropped like a loading screen, and Noah landed on a running track that looped back on itself, lanes glowing under his shoes.

"Start running," Circa said. "Count your laps."

He ran one loop. The scenery dimmed, went slow and foggy — quiet sleep. Then it brightened fast, colors sharper, like a cutscene starting — dream stuff. He hit the start line again just as his phone, somehow still in his pocket, buzzed with a timer: 90 minutes.

"Every lap's a cycle," Circa said. "Quiet sleep, then active dream sleep, back and forth, about **ninety minutes** each time, all night."

Noah spotted a shape lying in the grass mid-loop — a sleeping avatar, eyes darting under closed lids, body gone totally slack, like someone had dropped the controller input.

"Why's he limp like that?"

"Good catch. During dream sleep your brain's almost as busy as when you're awake — but your muscles go limp on purpose. Ragdoll mode. So you don't act out the dream where you're being chased by a dragon."

Noah grinned. "So sleep's got anti-cheat built in."

"Exactly backwards and exactly right," said Circa, and the track dissolved into something built like a gym.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Growth Spurt Gym
chapters.text:
He landed in a gym full of machines labeled in scrolling code, bars lifting themselves, nothing with actual weights. In the corner, a tall dial read GROWTH HORMONE, needle flat at zero.

"What's this?"

"Your body's upgrade station," Circa said. "It mostly turns on during the deepest stage of quiet sleep — no dreaming, just heavy, still sleep. That's one reason kids your age need more sleep than adults. More deep stage, more upgrades."

Noah eyed the dial. "So all those nights I fall asleep at 2 a.m. after one more match—"

"Fewer upgrades. The dial barely moves."

He stepped toward the controls anyway, found a switch, and pushed it to FULL DEEP SLEEP just to see. The needle swung hard right, bars across the gym lifting themselves twice as fast, lights flooding gold.

"See that?" Circa said. "That's what you're trading for one more match."

Noah didn't say anything, just watched the needle glow a while. Then he flicked it back toward normal and walked on, which was as close to an admission as Circa was going to get out of him tonight.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Mission Control
chapters.text:
Next room: a cramped control booth, dusty dials, one tiny glowing switchboard no bigger than a fingernail, mounted above two wires that crossed like an X.

"This," Circa said, "sits right above where your eye nerves cross. It's called the suprachiasmatic nucleus — a mouthful, so most people just call it the master clock. It decides when your whole body thinks it's day or night."

"Why's it so tiny?"

"Big decisions don't need big rooms."

Noah noticed a label under the switch: CIRCADIAN. "What's that mean?"

"Comes from Latin — circa, 'about,' and dies, 'day.' Your body's about-a-day clock."

He flicked the switch to NIGHT just to mess with it. Instantly the whole room dimmed, Circa's glow went sleepy, a yawn-animation looping on its face against its will.

"Hilarious," Circa said flatly. "Now flip it back before my whole operating system naps."

Noah flipped it back, laughing properly now. "So when I'm up till 3 scrolling, I'm basically hand-editing this thing's settings."

"Every single night," Circa said. "It notices. It just can't text you about it."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Patch Notes
chapters.text:
The booth opened into a vault, walls lined with scrolling green text like actual patch notes. A locked door read: NOBEL PRIZE, 2017.

"In **2017**, three scientists — **Jeffrey Hall, Michael Rosbash, and Michael Young** — won the Nobel Prize for finding the actual genes that keep your clock ticking," Circa said. "Basically, they found the source code."

"So the clock's not just a vibe. It's code."

"It's code. Older code, too — in **1958**, a scientist named **Aaron Lerner** isolated the hormone that makes you drowsy, called melatonin, out of a gland most people have never heard of. That's the chemical that tells your body it's bedtime."

A keypad blinked under the vault door, needing a gene-name password. Noah scanned the scrolling text, found three names repeating — Hall, Rosbash, Young — and typed them in order.

The door unbolted.

"Nice," Circa said, sounding almost impressed. "Most people just mash buttons."

"I read patch notes," Noah said. "Occupational habit."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Archive
chapters.text:
Inside: a hallway of shelves, each holding a glowing disc labeled with a date — his dates. One read YESTERDAY: GUITAR, 6:15 P.M.

"Sleep's where your brain files the day away," Circa said. "It sorts what matters into long-term memory. That riff you ran forty times at 6:15 — tonight's the night it either sticks or doesn't."

Down the hall, a smaller machine hissed and gurgled, flushing a thin mist out of a glass tube shaped like a brain.

"That's the glymphatic system," Circa said, catching Noah's look. "A nightly rinse cycle that flushes waste out of your brain while you sleep. Like clearing cache."

They passed a dusty shelf marked FREUD, 1899 — old film reels of melting clocks and staircases. "Some guy published a whole book back then saying dreams were secret wishes," Circa said. "Most scientists today think that's a stretch. Still, good trailer footage."

Noah reached for the GUITAR disc, hesitated, then slid it carefully onto a shelf marked SAVE, instead of leaving it on the floor where he'd found it.

"Nice instinct," Circa said.

"I don't lose saves," Noah said. "Learned that the hard way."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Eleven Days Awake
chapters.text:
The hallway spat them into a stark white room with a single red button on a pedestal: STAY AWAKE.

"In **1964**, a **seventeen-year-old named Randy Gardner**, from San Diego, stayed awake for about **eleven days** straight — a science-fair project that's still one of the longest documented stretches anyone's gone without sleep."

Noah whistled. "Eleven days. That's insane."

"It's also not something anyone should try again," Circa said. "Doctors are clear on that one — go without sleep and your mood, focus, and memory all tank fast. He didn't get a trophy. He got researchers studying him for years."

The red button pulsed, daring him.

Noah looked at it a long second, then stepped back from the pedestal entirely. "I'm good. I've got a boss fight tomorrow, and I'd like my brain for it."

"Smartest thing you've said all night," said Circa, and the button's glow died out, the pedestal folding away like it had never been a dare at all.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Sleep Arcade
chapters.text:
Last stop: an arcade floor of animal-shaped cabinets, each one a different high-score screen.

A cabinet shaped like a baby read 14–17 HRS/DAY. "Newborns," Circa said. "Nearly half of that's REM — dream sleep — while their brains build themselves."

Next to it, a dolphin cabinet showed one eye open. "Dolphins and some seals sleep with half their brain at a time. One side rests, the other stays alert, or just keeps them swimming."

A giraffe cabinet blinked UNDER 2 HRS. "Shortest sleepers of any big land animal. Quick standing naps."

A bat cabinet, by contrast, read 20 HRS. "Among the sleepiest mammals there are."

Noah pointed to a shuffling figure cabinet, eyes closed, walking in slow circles. "Sleepwalker?"

"Correct — and it happens during deep, dreamless sleep, not during a dream. So no, they're not acting one out."

Last cabinet: a tiny fruit fly, asleep mid-air. "Even bugs rest like this," Circa said. "Sleep's old. Really old."

Noah grinned at the row of cabinets. "High-score table for naps. I'd lose to the bat."

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Respawn
chapters.text:
The arcade folded back into static, static into green scanlines, and Noah blinked against the familiar dark of his own room, phone glowing faintly on the pillow beside him, screen still showing one last line of text.

YOU SPEND ABOUT A THIRD OF YOUR LIFE HERE. MAKE IT COUNT.

Circa's shape was almost gone now, just a thin outline in the screen's corner. "Same time tomorrow?"

"Depends if you let me finish my boss fight first."

"Depends if you let yourself finish your cycle first," Circa said, and faded into one last green blink before the screen went dark and ordinary.

Noah set the phone face-down on the nightstand, charger plugged in, which felt like a bigger deal than it should have. He pulled the blanket up, already running through riffs and respawn points in his head, half a patch note, half a dream.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow there was a guitar part to nail and a boss to beat, and both would go better after a real cycle or two.

facts.text: In 1953, Eugene Aserinsky and Nathaniel Kleitman at the University of Chicago discovered rapid eye movement (REM) sleep by watching a sleeping boy's eyes twitch under his eyelids.
A night's sleep is made of repeating cycles about 90 minutes long, moving between quiet non-REM sleep and active, dream-filled REM sleep.
During REM sleep the brain is almost as busy as when awake, but the body's muscles go limp so the sleeper cannot act out dreams.
The deepest non-REM stage triggers the most growth hormone release, one reason growing children need extra sleep.
A tiny brain region called the suprachiasmatic nucleus, just above where the eye nerves cross, works as the body's master clock for sleeping and waking.
'Circadian,' the body's roughly 24-hour clock, comes from Latin words meaning 'about a day.'
In 2017 the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine went to Jeffrey Hall, Michael Rosbash, and Michael Young for finding the genes that keep the circadian clock ticking.
The sleepy-time hormone melatonin was first isolated in 1958 by scientist Aaron Lerner's team, extracted from animal pineal glands.
Sleep helps the brain sort the day's experiences into long-term memories, so good sleep can help someone remember what they practiced or learned.
A nightly 'rinse cycle' called the glymphatic system flushes waste out of the sleeping brain.
In 1964, seventeen-year-old Randy Gardner of San Diego stayed awake about eleven days for a science-fair project, one of the longest documented periods without sleep.
Doctors do not recommend anyone try to break sleep-deprivation records, since going without sleep quickly harms mood, attention, and memory.
Newborns sleep about 14 to 17 hours a day in short bursts, nearly half of it in REM sleep.
Bottlenose dolphins and some seals sleep with only half their brain at a time, keeping one eye open to watch for danger or keep swimming.
Giraffes are among the shortest sleepers of any large mammal, sometimes under two hours a day in brief standing naps.
Some small bats sleep up to 20 hours a day, making them among the sleepiest mammals known.
Sleepwalking happens during deep non-REM sleep, not during dreaming, so sleepwalkers are usually not acting out a dream.
People spend roughly a third of their life asleep, based on typical nightly totals over a lifetime.
Nathaniel Kleitman, co-discoverer of REM sleep, is often called the father of modern sleep research.
In 1899, Sigmund Freud published 'The Interpretation of Dreams,' arguing dreams reveal hidden wishes; most of this specific theory is not accepted by scientists today.
Even fruit flies show sleep-like rest states, suggesting sleep is extremely ancient in life's history.
Chronic short sleep over months or years is linked by health researchers to problems with mood, learning, and the body's ability to fight illness.

story.title: Maya and the Great Space Race
story.subtitle: A bedtime splashdown among the stars

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Beeping Bathtub
chapters.text:
Maya lay in the bathtub, drawing a wobbly sailboat on the tile with a bath crayon.

It had been four whole nights since the big bridge hummed its last note, and Barnacle waved a flipper goodbye from the river. Tonight the water was just plain water. Or so she thought.

Then her little plastic rocket-boat went **BEEP. BEEP-BEEP. BEEP.**

Maya sat up fast. "Boats don't beep!"

The water began to swirl, glowing blue-white like a nightlight. Up popped a round, whiskery face. "All aboard, Maya!" said Barnacle the harbour seal, grinning his gap-toothed grin.

"That beeping sound," he said, "is really old. Long ago, on **October 4, 1957**, the Soviet Union — that's a country that doesn't exist anymore, but people there spoke Russian — launched a shiny ball called **Sputnik 1** into space. It was the first man-made thing ever to circle Earth, which just means go round and round it like a toy train on a track."

"How big was it?" Maya asked, dipping her crayon like a paintbrush.

"About the size of a beach ball," said Barnacle. "And it didn't do much. Just floated up there going **BEEP, BEEP, BEEP** on an ordinary radio, so people everywhere could listen in."

Maya grabbed her floating rocket-boat and held it to her ear. It beeped right along with the glowing water.

"That's the actual sound?" she said. "That's so weird. And so cool."

"Everyone thought so too," said Barnacle. "It scared some folks and thrilled everybody else, all at once. Two countries were racing to be first in space, and Sputnik had just won the first lap."

The water rose up around the tub in a shining ring, like a hula hoop made of light.

"Want to see where it went?" Barnacle asked.

Maya didn't even answer. She just grabbed the sides of the tub and held on.

**SPLOOSH!**

The bathroom disappeared. The bath crayon sailboat on the tile was the last thing she saw before the stars rushed in.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Laika's Big Loop
chapters.text:
Maya and Barnacle floated gently, surrounded by a soft dark sky full of tiny lights.

A little silver capsule, shaped like a goldfish bowl with wings, drifted past. Through its round window, Maya spotted something fuzzy and brown.

"Is that... a dog?" she gasped.

"Her name was **Laika**," said Barnacle. "On **November 3, 1957**, just a month after Sputnik, she became the first living creature to ever orbit Earth. She was small and brave, and the whole world cheered for her."

Maya pressed her hand against the glowing air, as close to the little dog as she could get. "Good girl," she whispered. "Good, good girl."

"People back home felt just like you do," said Barnacle softly. "They loved her for it."

On the other side of the sky, a second light blinked on, red, white, and blue.

"That one's new," said Maya, pointing. "What's that?"

"Good eye," said Barnacle. "The Americans were shocked that the Soviets kept winning. So on **October 1, 1958**, they started a brand new space team called **NASA**. That's just a short way of saying the group of people in America whose whole job is space."

A little rocket zoomed by with a toy-sized satellite riding on top.

"Their first satellite went up not long after," said Barnacle, "and it found something nobody expected floating around way up high — an invisible ring of space weather circling the whole planet."

Maya blinked. "You can't see weather!"

"Not with your eyes," grinned Barnacle. "But their instruments could. Pretty great for a first try, don't you think?"

Maya giggled and gave a little salute to the fuzzy dog drifting by. "Good job, Laika. Good job, everybody."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Gagarin's Giant Loop
chapters.text:
A loud **WHOOOOOSH** rattled the stars, and a silver rocket shot past so close that Maya's hair blew sideways.

"Whoa!" she laughed. "Who's driving that?"

"A pilot named **Yuri Gagarin**," said Barnacle, paddling after it. "On **April 12, 1961**, he climbed aboard a capsule called Vostok 1 and became the very first human being ever to go to space."

Maya watched the little rocket circle all the way around a glowing blue marble that looked an awful lot like Earth.

"How long did that take?" she asked.

"About **108 minutes**," said Barnacle.

Maya counted on her fingers, then gave up. "That's not even two whole movies!"

"Nope," said Barnacle. "One whole trip around the world, faster than you can finish popcorn."

Through the rocket's little round window, Maya could just make out a smiling face. She waved both arms as hard as she could.

"Do you think he can see me?" she asked.

"I think," said Barnacle, "wherever he is now, he'd be glad somebody's still waving."

The rocket gave a friendly wobble, almost like a wave back, before zooming off into the dark. Maya grinned so wide her cheeks hurt.

"Best. Loop. Ever," she said.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The President's Dare
chapters.text:
The stars thinned out, and a tall man in a dark suit appeared, standing on a little floating stage with a microphone.

"Why's there a grown-up just standing in space?" Maya whispered.

"That's **President Kennedy**," said Barnacle. "He ran the United States. On **May 25, 1961**, he stood up and made a big, bold promise."

The man's voice rolled out across the dark like thunder, even though he wasn't shouting. "We choose to land a man on the Moon," it echoed, "before this ten-year stretch — what grown-ups call a decade — is over."

Maya's mouth dropped open. "The actual Moon? Like, the one outside my window?"

"That very same Moon," said Barnacle, pointing at a pale round shape glowing in the distance.

"But nobody had ever done that," Maya said. "How did he even know it was possible?"

"He didn't, not for sure," said Barnacle. "That's what made it such a big dare. Sometimes the bravest thing you can do is promise something before you know exactly how."

Maya thought about the time she'd promised to swim a whole pool length without stopping, before she'd ever tried it even once.

"I get that," she said quietly. "I did it anyway. It just took practice."

"Just like this will," said Barnacle, nudging her shoulder with his nose. "Lots and lots of practice. Ready to watch some of it?"

Maya nodded so hard her teeth clicked.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Valentina's Turn
chapters.text:
A bright capsule zipped by, spinning gently like a top.

"Girls get to go too, right?" Maya asked suddenly. "It can't just be the boys having all the fun."

Barnacle's whiskers twitched into a smile. "Funny you should ask. On **June 16, 1963**, a woman named **Valentina Tereshkova** climbed aboard that very capsule, Vostok 6, and became the first woman ever to fly in space."

"What did she do before that?" Maya asked, paddling closer to peek through the window.

"She worked in a factory," said Barnacle. "Then she trained hard, and she went and circled the whole Earth, again and again and again."

Maya watched Valentina's capsule loop around the glowing Earth-marble, over and over, trailing a little sparkle each time like a skipping stone on a pond.

"She just kept going," Maya said, grinning. "Round and round and round."

"Just like that," said Barnacle. "Some people said girls couldn't do it. She went and circled the whole planet instead of arguing."

Maya pumped her fist in the air. "That's way better than arguing."

She waved as hard as she could, and for just a second, she was sure she saw a tiny wave wave back through the glass.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Floating Walk
chapters.text:
A hiss of air drifted past, and a figure in a puffy white suit floated right out of a capsule door, tethered by a long cord like a kite string.

Maya's eyes went huge. "He's just... floating? Outside the ship? In space?"

"That's **Alexei Leonov**," said Barnacle. "On **March 18, 1965**, he opened the hatch of his capsule, Voskhod 2, and became the first person ever to step outside into open space. Folks call that a spacewalk."

"Isn't that terrifying?" Maya asked, though she said it with a grin, not a worry.

"Maybe a little," said Barnacle. "But he had his tether, his suit kept him safe and breathing, and he floated right there for about **ten minutes** before climbing back in."

Maya watched Leonov tumble slowly, doing a lazy somersault with nothing below him but stars.

"I want to try that," she said, and tried a somersault of her own right there in the glowing dark. She spun clean around, giggling the whole way.

"Not bad," laughed Barnacle. "Though you'll want a spacesuit next time. It's a bit chilly out here."

"Worth it," said Maya, still spinning. "Totally worth it."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Photograph
chapters.text:
A quiet capsule drifted by, far bigger than the others, with a round window at its front.

"Shh," said Barnacle, for once not cracking a joke. "Watch this part."

Through the window, an astronaut lifted a camera. In **December 1968**, the Apollo 8 crew became the first people ever to circle the Moon, and one of them, **William Anders**, pointed his camera back the other way.

Maya followed his gaze.

There, hanging over the Moon's grey edge, was Earth. Blue and white and small, like a marble somebody had dropped and forgotten to pick up.

"That's... us?" Maya whispered. "That's everything? My whole house and the pool and everybody I know?"

"All of it," said Barnacle. "Right there in one little picture. People call it Earthrise."

Maya pulled her bath crayon from behind her ear, where it had somehow stayed tucked this whole time, and sketched the curve of it in the air, just to feel like she'd drawn it herself.

"It's so small," she said.

"And so is everyone on it," said Barnacle gently. "Which maybe makes it worth taking care of."

Maya tucked the invisible drawing against her chest, like she meant to keep it forever.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: One Giant Leap
chapters.text:
A huge rocket roared by, taller than anything Maya had ever seen, trailing fire like a comet.

"That one's enormous!" she shouted over the noise.

"That's Saturn V," said Barnacle. "Taller than the Statue of Liberty. It's carrying three astronauts to the Moon."

They followed it all the way down to a dusty grey ground. A ladder unfolded. A boot stepped down.

"On **July 20, 1969**," said Barnacle, "**Neil Armstrong** became the very first person to ever walk on the Moon. He said it was one small step for a man, one giant leap for mankind."

Maya watched him bounce across the dust in big, slow, floaty hops.

"The gravity's different there," she said. "He's basically flying!"

"Good thinking," said Barnacle. "A second astronaut, **Buzz Aldrin**, came down and bounced right along beside him. A third one, **Michael Collins**, stayed up above the whole time, flying the ship that would bring them all home."

"That seems lonely," said Maya. "Staying up there all by himself."

"Maybe," said Barnacle. "But somebody has to mind the boat while the others explore. Sound familiar?"

Maya thought of the times she'd held the rope while her family waded out from their little rowboat. "Yeah," she grinned. "Actually, it does."

She cupped her hands and shouted down at the little bouncing figures, even though she knew they couldn't hear her.

"ONE GIANT LEAP!" she yelled, and Barnacle yelled it right along with her.

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: The Scare and the Save
chapters.text:
The sky darkened, just a little, and the glow around them flickered.

"Uh oh," said Maya, grabbing Barnacle's flipper. "What's wrong?"

"In **1970**," said Barnacle, keeping his voice calm and steady, "a tank of oxygen — that's the air astronauts need to breathe — broke apart on a ship called Apollo 13, on its way to the Moon."

Maya's eyes went wide. "Were they okay?"

"Here's the good part," said Barnacle quickly. "Everyone on the ground worked together, day and night, and came up with a clever fix using things the astronauts already had on board. Every single one of those astronauts made it home safe."

Maya let out a breath she hadn't known she was holding. "That's such a relief."

"It sure was," said Barnacle. "Sometimes the bravest part of a story isn't the scary bit. It's everybody working together to fix it."

A little capsule drifted calmly past, splashing down into a wide, glittering sea below.

"They always land in water?" Maya asked, suddenly brightening. "Like boats?"

"Exactly like boats," said Barnacle, splashing his tail happily. "Big ships would come scoop them right up afterward. Space and water, Maya. Always more connected than people think."

Maya grinned her biggest grin of the whole night.

chapters.heading: Chapter 10: Splashdown Home
chapters.text:
The dark sky began to brighten, turning gold, then pink, then the familiar blue-white glow of the bathroom light.

"One more stop," said Barnacle, "before we head home."

Two spaceships drifted together, slow and careful, until their doors lined up.

"On **July 17, 1975**," said Barnacle, "an American ship and a Soviet ship docked together way up in orbit. The astronauts and cosmonauts opened their hatches and shook hands, right there in space."

"After racing each other the whole time?" Maya asked.

"That's how the whole race ended," said Barnacle. "Not with a winner and a loser. With a handshake."

Maya thought that sounded like exactly the right ending for a race that had started with a beeping ball and a very brave dog.

The glowing ring of light swirled around them again, pulling them gently down, down, down—

**SPLOOSH!**

Maya landed back in the bathtub with a splash, her bath crayon still tucked behind her ear, her little rocket-boat bobbing beside her, quiet now.

On the tile, her wobbly drawing of a sailboat had a tiny new addition next to it: a small, round Earth, blue and white, exactly like the one from the photograph.

"Did I draw that?" Maya whispered.

Barnacle winked one whiskery eye from the swirling water. "All aboard, Maya. Sleep tight."

He slipped beneath the surface with one last happy **SPLOOSH**, and the water went still and ordinary again.

Maya climbed out, wrapped herself in her towel, and carried her little rocket-boat all the way to bed.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Maya. All aboard for dreamland — SPLOOSH.

story.title: Eli and the Shortwave Century
story.subtitle: Eighteen years of rocket science, one dial at a time

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Beep in the Garage
chapters.text:
Eli was elbow-deep in a radio older than his dad when the thing started talking back.

He'd dragged the cracked **Zenith Transoceanic** shortwave set up to his room to rebuild it, mostly because the circuit diagram looked like a dare. His notebook sat open beside it, full of orbital math — the speed something needs to stay up, not just go up. That distinction was about to matter a lot.

The dial, which he hadn't touched, glowed cold green. Then came a sound he'd only heard in documentaries: a flat, steady **beep... beep... beep**.

He checked it against his own notes. "That's not random. That's got a rhythm."

The green light swallowed the room.

He landed on cold concrete under floodlights, beside a steel tower taller than his house. A man in a heavy coat glanced at him like new visitors showed up here all the time.

"You're hearing it right," the man said, nodding at a speaker pulsing the same beep. "**October 4, 1957.** We just put a ball in the sky."

The ball — barely **58 centimeters** wide, smaller than a beach ball — was already circling the planet, sending that beep to any radio on Earth tuned in right. Eli's own radio had caught the first satellite humans ever launched.

"Does anyone down here believe this yet?" Eli asked.

The man smiled. "Give it an hour."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Second Launch, Faster
chapters.text:
A month later — though for Eli it was five seconds — the green light dropped him somewhere colder.

Snow. Floodlights. And unmistakably, a bark.

"**November 3, 1957,**" said the same engineer, not even surprised to see him twice. "One month after the ball. This time we're sending up something that breathes."

Eli followed his pointing hand to a capsule being sealed, and inside it, a small dog with sharp ears, utterly calm about the whole thing.

"Laika," the engineer said. "First living creature to make it into orbit."

Eli ran the numbers on the capsule's path in his head. Orbit meant going fast enough sideways that you never come back down, not just going up and falling. "She's not just going up," he said slowly. "She's going fast enough sideways that she stays up there. That's what orbit even means."

The engineer looked at him with something like respect. "Most people just see a dog in a rocket. You're the first tourist who's shown his work."

Eli grinned, a little proud, as the capsule lifted with a roar that shook snow off the gantry.

"Good girl," he muttered, to a capsule already shrinking into the sky.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Needle That Wouldn't Stop
chapters.text:
The green light next time dropped him into a cramped control room full of men in short-sleeve shirts.

"**October 1, 1958,**" someone said, sliding a folder across a desk like it explained everything. "We just started an agency. NASA. Sputnik scared the whole country into building one."

Eli barely processed that before a scientist nearby started muttering at a dial. "Counter's maxed out. Again."

Eli looked over. It was a Geiger counter — a device that clicks faster the more radiation it senses — and the needle wasn't just high, it was pinned.

"**Explorer 1** went up January 31," the scientist said, rubbing his eyes. "First American satellite. Its counter keeps flat-lining at the top of its range, which makes no sense unless—"

"Unless there's way more radiation up there than you expected," Eli finished. "Like a whole belt of it."

The scientist froze, then laughed, short and disbelieving. "That's exactly what we're about to call it. The **Van Allen radiation belt** — a ring of charged particles trapped around Earth by its magnetic field. You just beat my boss to the punch by a week."

"I'll take partial credit," Eli said.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: One Hundred Eight Minutes
chapters.text:
Next stop smelled like jet fuel and nerves.

A rocket stood fueling on the pad, and beside it, a man in an orange suit laughed at something, utterly relaxed, like he was heading to the store instead of the edge of the atmosphere.

"**Yuri Gagarin,**" the engineer murmured, materializing again beside Eli. "**April 12, 1961.** First human being to leave the planet."

Eli did the math fast, the way he always did when nerves needed somewhere to go. Orbiting Earth once at that altitude took roughly — he scribbled on his arm — "**108 minutes.** Less than two hours to go all the way around the whole planet."

"Give or take," the engineer said. "He's not going to argue with your arithmetic. He'll be a little busy."

The rocket lit. The sound arrived a full second after the light did, a fact Eli had read about and never truly felt until the ground thumped his chest.

Gagarin was gone before the echo finished bouncing off the gantry.

"One hundred eight minutes," Eli repeated, grinning at an empty sky. "And he'll come back having been everywhere."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Up and Straight Back Down
chapters.text:
The next jump put Eli on a Florida beach, salt air and all.

A much smaller capsule sat on a smaller rocket. "This doesn't look like it's going to orbit," Eli said.

"It isn't," said a new voice, clipboard under his arm. "**Alan Shepard**, **May 5, 1961**. Up and straight back down. **Suborbital** — fast enough to touch space, not fast enough to stay there."

"So Gagarin circles the whole planet, and we just bounce," Eli said. "That's not exactly tied."

"Give us three weeks."

The green light resettled him before a podium and a crowd. A president Eli recognized from a textbook photo spoke.

"**May 25, 1961.**" He was daring the whole country to land a man on the Moon and bring him home safe — before the decade ended.

Eli did the math. Eight years. For something nobody had built yet.

"That's an insane deadline," he said.

"Most good physics," the clipboard man said, "starts as an insane deadline."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: No Ground Under Him
chapters.text:
"**June 16, 1963,**" the engineer announced, back again, like Eli's personal tour guide across a decade. "Watch this one."

Through a window Eli saw a woman in a flight suit settle into a capsule with the calm of someone who'd done harder things before breakfast.

"**Valentina Tereshkova,**" the engineer said. "Used to work in a textile factory. Today she's the first woman in space, orbiting Earth aboard Vostok 6."

Eli watched the capsule go, impressed less by the rocket than by the fact nobody down here seemed to think this was unusual at all.

The next jump was stranger. Eli found himself staring at a tiny window, and outside it, impossibly, a man — tethered, floating, surrounded by nothing.

"**March 18, 1965,**" the engineer said. "**Alexei Leonov.** First person to leave his spacecraft and just float there. A **spacewalk**. About **ten minutes**, suit and all, outside his capsule."

"No ground under him. No air. Just a line," Eli said, his stomach doing something complicated. "That's either the bravest or craziest thing I've ever seen."

"Why not both," said the engineer, and for once Eli didn't have a comeback.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Secret Name and the Tall Rocket
chapters.text:
The next landing site had a rocket so tall Eli tilted his whole body back to see the top.

"**363 feet,**" said a new voice, warmer than the others. "Taller than the Statue of Liberty. The **Saturn V**."

"Who builds something like this?"

"**Wernher von Braun** led the team," the man said. "Built rockets for Germany once, then came here and built this instead."

Eli's engineer from earlier jumps appeared at his shoulder, quieter than usual.

"**Sergei Korolev,**" he said. "Chief designer. Led every Soviet triumph tonight. Nobody outside this program knew his name while he was alive. Secret, until he died in **1966**."

Eli looked at him properly, wondering how much of this man's own name he'd never learn.

The Saturn V roared off toward the Moon — not landing yet, just circling it, **December 1968**, the first humans to see its far side with their own eyes.

A photograph reached Eli's hands later: Earth, blue and small, rising over a gray horizon. "Astronaut William Anders took that," the American said. "They call it Earthrise."

Eli held it like it might disappear.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Leap and the Fix
chapters.text:
"**July 20, 1969,**" the engineer said, and even he sounded like he was holding his breath.

Eli watched a ladder, a boot, then a footprint settle into gray dust untouched by anything alive.

"**Neil Armstrong,**" the American murmured. "First person to walk on the Moon. Called it one giant leap for mankind."

**Buzz Aldrin** came down next, and up in orbit, alone in the command module **Columbia**, **Michael Collins** circled the Moon by himself.

"Does anyone feel bad for Collins?" Eli asked. "He did all that work and didn't get to walk."

"Ask him," the engineer said. "He says he had the best seat in the house."

The next jump was rougher — an alarm blaring, a spacecraft shuddering.

"**1970,**" the American said fast. "Oxygen tank blew on the way to the Moon. **Apollo 13.**"

"Are they—"

"Alive. Engineers on the ground fixed it with parts the crew had onboard. They made it home."

Eli exhaled. "Insane luck or insane engineering."

"Both," the engineer said. "Between 1969 and 1972, **twelve** astronauts walked on the Moon across six missions. Thirteen just wasn't going to be the one that didn't come home."

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: The Handshake
chapters.text:
The last jump was the gentlest.

Two spacecraft, one American, one Soviet, drifted toward each other against the black, slow as two people meeting halfway across a room.

"**July 17, 1975,**" the engineer said. He looked, for the first time all night, like a man finishing something rather than starting it.

A hatch opened. An American hand reached through it. A Soviet hand took it.

"Eighteen years of racing," Eli said, "and it ends with a handshake?"

"It ends with two crews docking in orbit and shaking hands," the engineer said. "Call it whatever makes you smile more."

The green light rose up around Eli one last time, softer now, and the cold pad air turned back into the familiar smell of solder and dust.

He was on his bedroom floor. The Transoceanic sat where he'd left it, dial dark now, patient, like it had never glowed at all.

Eli looked down at his notebook. The orbital math he'd scribbled hours ago didn't look like homework anymore. It looked like a note Korolev or von Braun might have scrawled on the back of a napkin before any of this was history.

He picked up his soldering iron, found the radio's next broken joint, and got back to work.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow, he had a rocket of his own to design.

story.title: Hana and the Compass That Found the Titanic
story.subtitle: A true voyage from a Belfast shipyard to the bottom of the sea

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Keel in Belfast
chapters.text:
Hana lay on her bedroom floor with a world map spread flat under her elbows. She loved the thin blue lines that marked shipping routes — each one a story waiting to be read. Tonight she traced one slowly, from Southampton to New York.

On her shelf sat the brass compass she'd won at a school fair, dented and scratched, its needle never once pointing north. Tonight it spun three hard circles and stopped, aimed off the edge of her map into nothing at all.

Hana picked it up. It hummed low, like a foghorn far away, and the room filled with the smell of salt and wet rope.

"I'll always bring you home," the hum seemed to say. "Just hold on."

The paper map under her hands turned cold and damp. When she looked up, her bedroom was gone.

She stood inside a shed so big it had its own weather, under a steel skeleton taller than her school. Workers swarmed the scaffolding like ants on a whale.

"That," said a man beside her, chalk dust on his hands, "is the keel of the biggest ship this yard has ever laid." A **keel** is the long backbone a ship is built around — everything else gets added on top of it.

A board nearby read **31 March 1909**.

"That's today?" Hana asked.

"That's today," the foreman said. "Harland & Wolff shipyard, Belfast, Ireland. We're building her for the White Star Line. Her name is Titanic."

Hana touched a steel plate twice her height, warm from the workers' torches. "How long will she be, once she's finished?"

The foreman grinned. "Ask me in two years. Right now she's just bones."

The compass in Hana's pocket hummed again, impatient, like it already knew where this question was going to take them.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: She Floats
chapters.text:
The hum turned into a roar of cheering, and Hana found herself squeezed into a crowd on a riverbank. Two years had passed in one heartbeat.

Above her rose a finished hull, painted black, balanced on a long wooden ramp called a **slipway** — a slope built to slide a new ship down into the water for the very first time.

"She launches today," said a woman next to Hana, checking a pocket watch. "**31 May 1911.**"

Someone released a lever. Chains rattled loose. The hull groaned, shifted, and slid.

Hana held her breath as twenty-five thousand tons of ship found the river for the first time in its life.

**SPLOOOOSH!**

The water threw up a wave taller than the crowd. People screamed and laughed at once.

"SHE FLOATS!" Hana shouted, and nobody around her seemed to mind that a strange girl in pajama bottoms was shouting it loudest.

Later, standing on a dock official's clipboard list, Hana spotted a number and tapped it twice. "Is this her final length?"

The official checked. "**About 882 feet — 269 meters.** The largest ship in the whole world, right now, this year."

Hana tried to picture it and gave up. Some things are just too big to picture — you have to stand next to them instead.

"What happens to her now?" she asked.

"Now," the official said, closing the clipboard, "we finish her inside. Then she sails."

The compass warmed in Hana's pocket, already pulling her toward the next date.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Four Funnels, Two Sisters
chapters.text:
Hana landed on a crowded dock, band music playing somewhere, gulls wheeling overhead.

A huge painted sign read **SOUTHAMPTON**, and under it, a smaller chalked date: **10 April 1912**.

Titanic towered over the dock, finished at last, with four enormous funnels — the big smoke-pipes rising from her decks — standing in a row like chimneys for giants.

Hana counted them twice. Three trailed thin gray smoke into the sky. The fourth stood clean and empty.

"That one's not working," she said to a passing officer, pointing before he could stop her.

The officer laughed. "Sharp eyes. Only **three of the four funnels carry real smoke.** The fourth is mostly there to look grand."

"So it's... decoration?"

"A very large, very expensive decoration," he agreed.

Inside the first-class lounge, Hana found a framed painting of three nearly identical ships lined up side by side.

"Those are her sisters," the officer said, following her gaze. "Titanic is the second of three — **Olympic and Britannic** are the other two."

Hana grinned. "I didn't know ships had sisters."

"This family just happens to be enormous," he said.

A horn blasted, long and deep, and the whole dock seemed to lean forward. Ropes thick as Hana's arm splashed into the water, and Titanic began, very slowly, to move.

Somewhere below her feet, engines the size of houses were just getting started.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Sixteen Rooms and Twenty Boats
chapters.text:
Below decks, a crew member named Thomas was showing visitors the ship's safety features, and Hana tagged along, notebook brain fully switched on.

"The hull is divided into **sixteen separate compartments**," Thomas explained, "each one sealed off by doors that shut tight, so water can't spread from one into the next." People were calling the design **watertight**, meaning no water could cross between them.

"So if one fills with water," Hana said slowly, working it out, "the others stay dry, and she still floats?"

"Exactly. Some newspapers have started calling her unsinkable."

Hana frowned at the word. It sounded like a dare to the ocean.

Up on the open deck, she found rows of white lifeboats hanging from metal arms. She started counting them, finger moving along the row, the way she counted pins on her bedroom map.

"Twenty," she said finally. "How many people fit in twenty boats?"

Thomas checked a clipboard. "Altogether, the boats carry **about 1,178 people.**"

Hana looked up at the decks stacked above her, crowded with passengers waving at the dock. "That's not everyone on this ship, is it?"

Thomas didn't answer right away. "The rules at the time only counted lifeboats by the size of the ship, not by how many people were aboard," he said carefully. "It's something people are already starting to question."

Hana looked at the boats again, then at the crowd, and said nothing more. Some questions you just have to carry with you.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Night the Sea Went Quiet
chapters.text:
The compass pulled, and the deck under Hana's feet turned icy cold.

The sea had gone strangely still, flat as glass, stars scattered thick overhead with no moon at all. Hana shivered, though she knew — somehow, the compass had told her without words — that nothing here could actually touch her.

A lookout's bell clanged twice, sharp in the silence.

"Iceberg, right ahead!"

The ship shuddered, a long low grinding Hana felt through her shoes more than heard. It was **about 11:40 p.m. on 14 April 1912.**

On the bridge, a man in uniform gave calm, quiet orders. "That's Captain Edward Smith," murmured a steward nearby. "Most experienced captain the White Star Line has."

Upstairs in a small radio room, two men in headphones tapped furiously at a brass key. "That's Jack Phillips and Harold Bride," the steward said. "Sending for help."

They were using **wireless** — sending messages through the air with no wires at all, using an old distress call, **CQD**, and a newer one just coming into use, **SOS**.

Hana leaned close to the door, heart thudding, and watched the dots and dashes click out into the dark.

"Will someone hear them?" she whispered.

The steward nodded. "Ships for miles around are listening tonight."

Out on deck, crew moved calmly between lifeboats, helping passengers climb in, voices low and steady. Nobody ran. Nobody screamed. The night stayed quiet, and somewhere far off, that quiet was already carrying a message for help across the water.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Band Played On
chapters.text:
Hana found the ship's band tucked near the grand staircase, instruments out, playing steady and bright as if nothing at all were wrong.

"That's Wallace Hartley," the steward said, nodding toward the violinist leading them. "People who were there later said the band kept playing, right to the end, to keep everyone calm."

"Is that true?" Hana asked.

"Nobody agrees anymore on exactly which songs," the steward admitted. "It might be a little bit of a legend by now. But survivors really did remember hearing music that night, and that part keeps turning up in every story people tell."

Hana decided she liked that kind of true — the kind that gets a little polished by time but keeps its shine.

Near a lifeboat, a woman in a fur-trimmed coat was helping other passengers climb aboard, then grabbed an oar herself.

"That's Margaret Brown," the steward said. "Everyone just calls her Molly. She rowed half the night herself and wouldn't stop arguing with anyone who told her to sit still."

"They'll call her the Unsinkable Molly Brown," Hana said, remembering something she'd read once, long ago, in a book about ships.

A small commotion near the rail caught her eye — a woman tucking not one but two small **Pomeranian** dogs, fluffy and shivering, inside her coat before stepping into a lifeboat.

Hana smiled despite the cold. Of all the things to remember from a night like this, two rescued dogs felt like exactly the right size of hope to hold onto.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Carpathia's Run
chapters.text:
Hana watched from the deck rail as the last lifeboats pulled away into the dark, oars dipping quietly into black water.

She knew, without being told, that this part of the story ended gently: the ship sank at **around 2:20 a.m. on 15 April 1912**, less than three hours after the iceberg, and the people in the boats drifted, cold and waiting, until the sky turned gray.

Then, far off, a light.

"That's the Carpathia," the steward said, voice warm with relief. "She heard the wireless call and turned around in the night, steaming as fast as her engines could push her."

One by one, the lifeboats rowed toward the light, and the Carpathia's crew hauled survivors up her sides, wrapped them in blankets, poured hot drinks into cold hands.

Hana felt her chest loosen for the first time in two chapters.

The compass hummed, and the gray morning blurred into something else — offices, newspapers, men in suits arguing over charts and rulebooks.

"After that night," a different voice explained, "two things changed everywhere, forever. Ships started patrolling the North Atlantic every spring, watching for icebergs and warning everyone nearby — they call it the **International Ice Patrol.**"

"And the lifeboats?" Hana asked.

"A new rule, called **SOLAS**, said every ship must carry enough lifeboats for every single person aboard. No exceptions, ever again."

Hana thought of the twenty boats she'd counted, and the question she'd carried since. Someone, finally, had answered it properly.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Finder of Lost Ships
chapters.text:
The compass spun hard, past decades, until Hana stood on the deck of a small research ship, salt spray stinging her cheeks, screens glowing in a dim cabin nearby.

"**1 September 1985,**" read a date on a monitor.

A man with a steady, excited voice leaned over a screen showing gray shapes crawling across the seafloor. "That's Robert Ballard," the steward said — he'd followed her through every date somehow, same steady presence. "An **oceanographer** — a scientist who studies the sea — he's been searching for Titanic for years."

On the screen, a shape sharpened: a boiler, huge and round, sitting alone on the mud.

"FOUND HER!" someone shouted, and the whole cabin erupted.

Hana leaned close. "Where is she?"

"**About 370 miles off Newfoundland, Canada,**" Ballard said, grinning at his screens, "**resting about 12,500 feet down** — split into two main pieces on the seafloor."

Hana thought of the ship she'd watched slide down a slipway, funnels smoking, band playing, lifeboats loading. All of it, still down there, keeping its own kind of quiet.

The compass hummed its lowest note yet — home.

Hana's bedroom floor came back under her knees, map still spread out, compass warm in her palm.

She thought of a museum shaped like a ship's bow that she'd read about once, opened a hundred years after the sinking, and a movie everyone always seemed to be watching on rainy Sundays, and glass cases somewhere full of old shoes and dinner plates pulled up gently from the dark.

She traced the shipping route on her map one more time, from Southampton toward New York, and this time she knew every single mile of it.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow, she had a hundred more routes on that map left to trace.
