story.title: Ben and the Pixel Block of Game History
story.subtitle: A bedtime adventure through the history of video games.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Glowing Cube
chapters.text:
Ben was drawing a pixel art creeper on his tablet, all blocky and green, with his Minecraft world glowing on the screen beside it. Suddenly the tablet flickered black, then green, then black again.

On his shelf, a little cube he'd built from spare bricks started glowing that exact same green. Ben poked it. The cube popped open like a treasure chest.

Out hopped a tiny pixel creature, all square edges, blinking two blocky eyes. "LOADING... FRIEND FOUND," it beeped. "I'm Blip. Want to see where video games came from?"

Ben grinned. "Like, the very first one ever?"

"PRESS START," said Blip. The air went fuzzy and green, and then Ben wasn't in his room anymore.

He stood in a humming room full of machines taller than a fridge, wires everywhere. A man in a white coat squinted at a round glowing screen. "That's an **oscilloscope**," Blip explained, "a machine that draws lines of light to show how electricity wiggles."

The man was **William Higinbotham**, a scientist at a lab called **Brookhaven**, back in **1958**. He'd turned his wiggly-line machine into a game: two players batting one glowing dot back and forth, like tennis.

"Can I try?" Ben asked. The scientist handed him a box with one knob and one button. Ben turned the knob. The glowing dot arced over the little net. BOING!

"That's **Tennis for Two**," Blip said, "one of the very first video games ever played."

Ben grinned so wide it nearly broke his own pixel-art rules. "Oldest game I've ever played," he said, "and it doesn't even have graphics."

Blip blinked. "Give it time."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Closet-Sized Computer
chapters.text:
Blip's cube hummed, and the room dissolved into somewhere colder, full of blinking lights. A computer the size of a closet took up an entire wall.

"This is a **PDP-1**," Blip said. "Back then, a computer filled a whole room, not a pocket."

A college student with messy hair was typing fast, muttering numbers. A sign on the wall said **1962**. "What are you building?" Ben asked.

The student spun around, grinning. "Two spaceships. They shoot at each other. Whoever wins, wins!" He flicked a switch. Two tiny triangle ships appeared on a round screen, spinning around a blinking dot of gravity.

Ben's jaw dropped. "That's basically a space version of dodgeball!" He grabbed a spare switch panel. "Can I fly one?"

The student, **Steve Russell**, nodded. Ben nudged his ship left, dodging the gravity dot, zipping past the other ship.

"I WON MY FIRST SPACE BATTLE!" Ben yelled, loud enough that Blip's cube-eyes wobbled with laughter.

"That game is called **Spacewar!**," Blip said. "Steve Russell and his friends built it right here, in **1962**."

Ben patted the warm, humming computer like a dog. "Good game, old buddy." The computer didn't answer, but a few lights blinked, which Ben decided counted as agreeing.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Box That Lived in a TV
chapters.text:
The green fuzz dropped them into a cluttered workshop, wires everywhere, a fat old television in the corner. A man with round glasses soldered something onto a board.

"Who's that?" Ben whispered.

"**Ralph Baer**," said Blip. "People call him the father of video games, because he had a wild idea: what if your regular TV could play games?"

Ben looked at the old TV, then at Ralph's tangled box of wires. "Does it even work?"

Ralph clipped in one more wire and flipped a switch. Two white squares appeared on the screen with a dotted line between them. "Watch," he said, handing Ben a dial.

Ben spun it. One square moved up. "It's like... TV Pong already!" he said.

Ralph chuckled. "Close. This is my **prototype** — my very first test version. I call it the **Brown Box**, built in the late 1960s."

Blip zipped them ahead, to a toy store shelf. A box sat there, pictured with a family gathered around their TV, labeled **Magnavox Odyssey**.

"In **1972**," Blip said, "Ralph's invention became this: the very first video game system you could buy for your own home."

Ben held the box like treasure. "So before this," he said slowly, "nobody could play games on their own TV. Ever."

"Nobody," Blip agreed.

Ben hugged the box to his chest. "Ralph Baer basically invented game night."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Machine Full of Quarters
chapters.text:
A blink of green light landed them inside a noisy, dim arcade, buzzing with beeping machines. One cabinet by the door had a simple black-and-white screen: two paddles, one bouncing ball. "PONG," read the sign.

"Two guys built this," Blip said. "**Nolan Bushnell** and **Ted Dabney**. They started a company called **Atari**, and in **1972**, this game hit arcades."

Ben dropped in a coin and grabbed the paddle knob. BLIP. BLOP. He volleyed the little square ball back and forth, score ticking up.

"This game is so simple," Ben said, "but I can't stop playing it."

"Funny you say that," Blip said. "There's a story that one early Pong machine got so popular, so fast, that it jammed completely full of quarters and just stopped working."

Ben blinked. "Wait — it broke from being TOO popular?"

"That part might be a little bit of an exaggeration," Blip admitted, "but it tells you how wild people went for this game."

Ben patted the machine gently. "Don't worry, buddy. I'll only put in one quarter." He paused. "I don't actually have a quarter."

Blip's cube-face did something that looked suspiciously like a smirk. "PRESS START anyway," it said.

Ben pressed. The ball bounced. Somewhere, Nolan Bushnell would have been proud.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Swap the Cartridge, Save the World
chapters.text:
Next they landed in a bedroom from long ago, a kid hunched over a TV with a strange plastic box plugged in. The kid slid a flat plastic brick into a slot. CLUNK.

"That's a **cartridge**," Blip said. "Instead of one built-in game, you swap cartridges to play something new."

Ben's eyes lit up. "That's like swapping tools in my inventory!" He grabbed a cartridge from a stack and clicked it in. A new game flashed onto the screen.

"This is the **Atari 2600**," Blip said, "released in **1977**."

Before Ben could try another one, the air rippled, and they stood in a packed, glowing arcade. Rows of little pixel aliens marched across a screen, slowly, menacingly, step by step.

A man adjusted dials nearby. "**Tomohiro Nishikado**," Blip said. "He made this game, called **Space Invaders**, in **1978**. It became a worldwide craze."

Ben studied the aliens, blocky and square. "I could totally draw these," he said, grabbing a scrap of paper and sketching one in seconds — pointy legs, round eyes.

Tomohiro peered over. "Not bad," he said. "Mine took longer."

Ben beamed, tucking the sketch into his pocket like a souvenir. "Pixel art before pixel art was even a thing."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Pizza, a Crash, and a Buried Treasure
chapters.text:
The scene shifted to a sunny office, where a man stared at a round yellow shape on his drawing table, a wedge missing from one side.

"What's that supposed to be?" Ben asked.

"**Toru Iwatani**," Blip said. "People say he got the idea from looking at a pizza with a slice taken out of it. Nobody's completely sure that's exactly how it happened, but it's a fun story, and it stuck."

Ben grinned. "Pac-Man is a pizza. I'm never eating pizza the same way again." He grabbed the controller and gobbled little dots across the maze, dodging four colorful ghosts. "In **1980**, this became huge," Blip added.

The lights flickered, and suddenly shelves of games stretched endlessly, most of them looking rushed and sloppy. "In **1983**," Blip said, "so many bad games got made so fast that people stopped buying them. Sales dropped a lot. It's called the video game **crash**."

Ben frowned. "That sounds sad."

"It got better," Blip said gently. "But first — there's a story that a bunch of unsold cartridges, games nobody wanted, got buried in a giant dirt pile out in the desert, in **New Mexico**."

Ben's eyes went wide. "Buried? Like treasure?"

"Sort of. In **2014**, people actually dug there and found the cartridges were really there."

Ben grabbed an imaginary shovel. "I would've dug that up in five seconds. I've got Minecraft hands."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Jumping Plumber and the Falling Blocks
chapters.text:
A cheerful jingle rang out as Ben landed in front of a glowing screen showing a mustached man in overalls, running through green pipes and brick blocks.

"No way," Ben said. "That's Mario."

"**Shigeru Miyamoto** designed him," Blip said. "In **1985**, this game, **Super Mario Bros.**, came packed with a new game system called the **NES**, and it brought video games roaring back after the crash."

Ben grabbed the controller and jumped Mario clean over a pit. "This feels like building in Minecraft," he said. "Jump, grab, jump again."

The scene shifted again, colder this time, a computer glowing in a quiet office. Blocky shapes drifted down the screen, stacking into neat rows.

"**Alexey Pajitnov** made this one," Blip said, "at a computer center in **Moscow**, in **1984**. It's called **Tetris**."

Ben watched a long shape fall and slid it sideways just in time. The row filled and vanished. "It's basically a block puzzle," he said. "I'm WAY too good at this."

Alexey raised an eyebrow, impressed. Ben shrugged modestly. "I build with blocks for a living. Well. For fun. Same thing."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Blue Blur, Shiny Discs, and Wired-Up Friends
chapters.text:
A streak of blue zipped past so fast Ben barely saw it. "Whoa, what was THAT?"

"**Sonic the Hedgehog**," Blip said. "Sega made him in **1991** to race against Mario, speed against speed."

Ben grabbed the controller and zoomed Sonic through loops, laughing at how fast the screen blurred by. "He's basically built for people with no patience," Ben said. "I love him."

Next came a quieter room, where a shiny circle disc spun inside a machine. "That's a **CD**," Blip explained. "It holds way more pictures and sound than a cartridge could."

"**Sony** used these in their new system, the **PlayStation**, starting in **1994**," Blip said. Ben held the disc up to the light, rainbow colors swirling across it. "It's like a tiny spinning universe."

The scene shifted once more: a basement crowded with kids, computers lined up on folding tables, wires running between every machine.

"This is a **LAN party**," Blip said. "Everybody plugs their computers together with wires so they can all play the same game at once."

"What game?" Ben asked.

"**Doom**," said Blip, "from **1993**. It helped make playing together like this popular."

Ben helped plug in one last cable, and the screens all lit up together. The whole room cheered. "Teamwork," Ben said, "but with extension cords."

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: The Game That Was Already His
chapters.text:
The fuzz swirled, and Ben landed in a bright living room, a family waving their arms at a TV while little characters on screen copied every move.

"That's the **Wii**," Blip said. "In **2006**, Nintendo made controllers you just wave around, and the game watches you move."

Ben swung an invisible tennis racket, and on screen, his character did the same. "This is like gym class, but fun," he said.

Then the green light shifted one last time, and Ben froze. Blocky green hills. Square trees. A pixel sun.

"Wait," Ben said. "This is MY game."

"**Minecraft**," Blip said, "made by **Markus Persson** in **2011**. It went on to become the best-selling video game ever."

Ben grinned so hard his cheeks hurt. "I knew it was good. I didn't know it was THAT good."

Last of all, Blip led him into a quiet museum room, glass cases glowing softly, old game cartridges and controllers lined up like treasures. "The **World Video Game Hall of Fame**," Blip said. "It opened in **2015**, in Rochester, New York, so people never forget where games came from."

Ben pressed his hand to the glass. "History really is just a really long save file."

Then the museum blurred to green, to black, and Ben blinked — and he was back on his bedroom floor, tablet glowing softly beside him. His pixel-art creeper was still half-drawn. The toy cube on his shelf had gone quiet, dark, ordinary again.

Except for one thing: a tiny pixel badge, shaped like a trophy, sat glowing faintly on the carpet. Ben picked it up and set it carefully next to his controller.

"Night, Blip," he whispered to the cube. It gave one last tiny blink.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Ben. Good game, sleep tight.

story.title: Theo and the Glitch in the Baseplate
story.subtitle: One ball problem, sixty years in the making

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Glitch in the Baseplate
chapters.text:
Theo was lying on his bedroom floor, laptop balanced on a pillow, deep in Roblox Studio.

He was building a soccer stadium, a whole stand of seats and a working scoreboard, and the only thing left to fix was the ball.

Every time he kicked it, it floated. Like it had forgotten gravity existed.

"Come ON," he said, mashing at the script window. "Just bounce normal."

He tried a shortcut he'd found buried in a forum, a secret key combo nobody really admitted to using. The screen flashed black, then green, like a computer screen from decades before he was born — except this one had never been in his room before tonight.

A cursor blinked in the corner. Then it grew arms. Then legs. Then it waved.

"Finally," said the small green sprite. "Someone with a ball problem."

Theo sat up so fast he knocked his water bottle over. "Did my laptop just... talk?"

"I'm Glitch," said the sprite, hands on its blocky hips. "I live in the code. Every game ever made, I've seen the inside of it. You want your ball to bounce right? I know a guy. Well. Knew a guy."

The screen folded outward like a page turning, and Theo found himself staring at a glowing green window the size of a wall — an **oscilloscope**, a machine scientists once used to watch wobbly lines of electricity dance across a screen.

On it, a bright dot arced over a line, like a tiny tennis ball clearing a net.

"In **1958**," Glitch said, "a scientist named **William Higinbotham** built this. He called it **Tennis for Two**. It ran on a lab machine at **Brookhaven National Laboratory**, and people lined up around the hallway for a turn."

Theo watched the dot bounce, again and again, the same curve every time.

"Wait," he said. "That's not random. That's a curve. He's got a gravity number programmed in there. Same as I'm trying to do."

Glitch grinned, all pixels. "Took the actual scientists less time to figure that out than it took you."

"Hey."

"I'm kidding. Mostly."

Theo reached toward the glowing dot without thinking, and the whole scene swallowed him, screen and all, like falling through a loading bar.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Duel on the PDP-1
chapters.text:
Theo landed somewhere that hummed.

Rows of machines the size of refrigerators blinked at him, lights ticking on and off like a scoreboard that couldn't make up its mind.

"Where—"

"**1962**," said Glitch, appearing on his shoulder like a tiny mascot. "Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Smart people. Rough haircuts."

A student hunched over a round screen, flipping switches on a panel the size of a kitchen counter. Two little ships spun around a glowing dot in the middle, shooting at each other.

"That's a **PDP-1**," Glitch said. "A whole computer, the size of a fridge, with less memory than your phone's camera roll."

"Who's winning?" Theo asked.

"**Steve Russell**, and some friends of his. They wrote the whole game themselves, from nothing. It's called **Spacewar!** Two ships, two players, no mercy."

Theo leaned in close. The student's ship kept drifting too near the middle dot and getting yanked off course.

"He keeps dying because of that star in the middle," Theo said. "It's pulling his ship in. Like actual gravity."

"It is gravity," Glitch said. "They coded it in on purpose. Made the game harder on purpose, which, I'll be honest, is a very soccer-coach thing to do."

"Tell him to use the star instead of fighting it," Theo said. "Swing around it. Like cutting around a defender instead of running straight at them."

Glitch floated down and whispered something nobody else in the room heard. The student blinked, adjusted his grip, and swung his ship in a wide arc around the star — coming out right behind the other ship.

A tinny beep rang out. Somebody groaned. Somebody else cheered.

"Okay," Theo said, "I want a turn."

"You'll get plenty," Glitch said. "This is only stop two of a very long night."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Box That Played on Your TV
chapters.text:
The hum faded into the quiet buzz of a cluttered workshop. Wires covered every surface, and a television sat propped on a wheeled cart.

A man with thick glasses and a soldering iron didn't even glance up when Theo's sneakers landed on the floor beside him.

"He can't see you," Glitch said. "Ghosts don't surprise engineers. Mostly because engineers don't look up."

Theo picked up a small white box with two dials on the front. "What's this?"

"Say hello to **Ralph Baer**," Glitch said. "Late **1960s**. He wants you to play games on your actual television. Not a lab machine, not a university building. Your living room."

Baer connected the box to the TV. Two white squares appeared, chasing each other through the static.

Theo turned one of the dials. His square jumped left.

"Oh — that's a controller," Theo said. "That's literally just a controller."

"Everybody needs a first one," Glitch said. "He called this prototype **the Brown Box**. Later, it got sold under a different name."

A cardboard sign went up over a stack of boxes on a nearby shelf: MAGNAVOX ODYSSEY, 1972.

"The **first home video game console** anyone could actually buy and carry home," Glitch said. "**1972**. Before this, games lived in labs and university buildings. After this, games lived on your couch, same as you."

Theo turned the dial again, chasing the other square around the screen, grinning when his finally caught it.

"This is basically the great-great-grandfather of my controller," Theo said, holding up his imaginary gamepad hands.

"Your mom's going to ask why there's a dusty TV showing up in your dreams," Glitch said.

"She's not going to believe any of this," Theo said. "Honestly, neither do I."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Quarters by the Bucket
chapters.text:
Theo landed beside a glowing cabinet in a dim room full of booth seats, bleeps rattling out of a tinny speaker.

A black-and-white screen showed two paddles and a square dot — a ball — bouncing between them, back and forth, back and forth.

"**Pong**," Glitch said. "**1972**. Made by two guys named **Nolan Bushnell** and **Ted Dabney**, who'd just started a brand-new company called **Atari**."

Theo watched two players volley the little square, both grinning like it was the best thing either of them had ever seen.

"That's basically soccer," he said. "Just — flatter. And way slower."

"Everything starts somewhere," Glitch said.

A waiter tried to feed the machine a coin, and the slot jammed, spitting quarters onto the floor in a little silver waterfall.

"Whoa," Theo said. "It's stuffed."

"That's the story, anyway," Glitch said. "People say an early Pong machine once got so packed with quarters that it actually stopped working. That one's probably stretched taller than it really happened, but it tells you how fast people fell for this thing."

Theo knelt and peered into the coin slot. "You'd need a way bigger bucket in there. Or someone to empty it more."

"They figured that out pretty quickly too," Glitch said. "Mostly because of nights exactly like this one."

A line of people had already formed behind them, coins ready, bouncing on their heels.

"GAME ON!" someone shouted from the back of the line, and Theo laughed, because it sounded exactly like something he'd yell at a friend for hogging the controller too long.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Swap the Cartridge
chapters.text:
Theo landed in a living room with shag carpet and a wood-paneled television in the corner.

A console sat beneath it, a plastic rectangle slotted into the top like a drawer waiting to be opened.

"The **Atari 2600**," Glitch said. "**1977**. Before this, machines like the Odyssey came with their one game already built in. This one swaps."

Theo pulled the cartridge halfway out and turned it over in his hands. "Wait — so it's one machine, but different games, and you just change the cartridge? That's basically what I do when I pick a different game inside Roblox. Same device, totally different world."

"Exactly that," Glitch said. "Except you don't even need to get off the couch."

Theo slid in a different cartridge, and the screen flickered to life: rows of blocky alien shapes marching slowly downward, a tiny cannon waiting at the bottom.

"**Space Invaders**," Glitch said. "**1978**. A designer named **Tomohiro Nishikado** made it for a company called Taito, and it kicked off an arcade craze across the whole world."

Theo grabbed the joystick, firing up at the descending rows, dodging their return shots, grinning as the aliens sped up the closer they got to the bottom of the screen.

"They get faster," he said. "That's mean. That's a good kind of mean."

"The fewer invaders left standing, the faster the rest move," Glitch said. "Nishikado built that in on purpose, same as the gravity back in Spacewar. Turns out making a game a little unfair, in just the right spot, makes people want another quarter."

Theo cleared the last alien with one shot and pumped his fist like he'd just scored in stoppage time.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Buried Treasure
chapters.text:
Before the desert, there was pizza.

"**1980**," Glitch said, pointing at a new arcade cabinet, a yellow dot chomping its way through a maze of white dots. "Designer named **Toru Iwatani** made this one for a company called Namco. Story goes, he looked down at a pizza missing a slice and got an idea."

"**Pac-Man**," Theo said. "Obviously. Everyone knows Pac-Man."

"Everyone knows Pac-Man because of what happened next, actually," Glitch said, and the scene shifted — fast, like a loading screen — to a dusty stretch of desert in New Mexico.

A bulldozer pushed dirt over a long trench full of broken plastic cartridges.

"What happened?" Theo asked, quieter now.

"**1983**," Glitch said. "Stores had gotten flooded with games — way too many, way too rushed, way too bad. People stopped trusting the shelf. The whole North American games business shrank, hard."

Theo crouched by the edge of the trench. Boxes with E.T. printed on the front poked out of the loose dirt.

"They buried the games?" he said. "Like — actually buried them? In the ground?"

"Story says so," Glitch said. "Unsold cartridges, dumped in a landfill right here. People thought it was just a tall tale for thirty years — until diggers actually found them, in **2014**."

Theo picked up a crushed cartridge case and turned it over in his hands. "So too many bad games, all at once, and the whole thing just — broke?"

"Pretty much."

"That's exactly what happens when a Roblox game's reviews get flooded with junk," Theo said. "People stop trusting any of it, even the good ones."

"Huh," Glitch said. "Never thought of it that way. You should write that down somewhere."

"I will," Theo said. "Right after we leave the desert."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: A Plumber and Some Falling Blocks
chapters.text:
The desert folded away like a browser tab closing, and a toy-store shelf appeared instead.

Bright gray boxes lined the shelf, stamped with letters: NINTENDO ENTERTAINMENT SYSTEM.

"**1985**," Glitch said. "Nintendo brought the whole American games business back from the brink with this one. **The NES**. And they didn't launch it alone."

A small screen beside the console showed a mustached man in overalls running across colorful blocks, hopping clean over a turtle.

"**Super Mario Bros.**," Glitch said. "A designer named **Shigeru Miyamoto** made it, same year. A plumber named Mario. Still the most famous character games have ever produced."

Theo grabbed the controller and jumped Mario over a gap, then another, timing each leap a half-second early, the same trick he used lining up headers on the soccer field.

"They bundled the game right into the box with the console," Glitch said. "Buy the machine, Mario's already inside. People could barely say no."

"Smart," Theo said. "Give people the best thing you've got, free, right at the start. Hook them."

Glitch tugged him sideways, past a different glowing screen — black background, falling shapes stacking up toward the top.

"**1984**, a year earlier, actually," Glitch said. "Moscow. A scientist named **Alexey Pajitnov** made this one at a computer center. **Tetris**."

Theo watched the blocks fall and spin, and jammed the rotate button just in time to slot an L-shaped piece neatly into a gap.

"It's just satisfying," he said. "There's no story, no character, it's just — pieces fitting where they're supposed to."

"That's the whole game," Glitch agreed. "Sometimes that's enough."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Blue, Fast, and Wired Together
chapters.text:
A blue blur shot across the screen so fast Theo nearly missed it entirely.

"**1991**," Glitch said. "Sega needed a mascot fast enough to compete with Mario, so they built one that was, well, fast. **Sonic the Hedgehog**."

Theo took the controller, and Sonic rocketed through loops so quickly the background blurred into streaks of color.

"Okay, that one's definitely for people who think Mario's too slow," Theo said.

Next came a gray console with a slot that didn't look anything like a cartridge slot — flat, round, shiny.

"**PlayStation**, **1994**," Glitch said. "Sony's first console. It used **CDs** instead of cartridges, which meant way more room for video and sound. Massive jump."

Theo held the disc up to the light. "Like trading a flip phone for a smartphone, basically."

"Not a bad way to put it."

In the next room, a row of chunky computers sat wired together, cables snaking across a carpeted floor, a bunch of teenagers hunched over keyboards, shouting across the room at each other.

"**1993**, a game called **Doom** got people doing this," Glitch said. "Connecting computers together with cables so a whole group of players could play each other at once, all in the same room. People called it a **LAN party**."

"That's just a Roblox server," Theo said, "except you had to physically carry your computer to somebody's house to join one."

"Basically," Glitch said. "You've got it easier now. No cables. No hauling a monitor up a flight of stairs."

"I believe you," Theo said, eyeing the tangle of wires at his feet. "I believe you completely."

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Back to the Baseplate
chapters.text:
A white console with a slim white remote sat under a TV in a cozy living room, a grandmother and a kid both holding one, both laughing.

"**2006**," Glitch said. "Nintendo's **Wii**. You didn't press buttons so much as swing your whole arm like you meant it."

Theo picked one up and swung it like a tennis racket, and on-screen, a cartoon character mirrored him exactly, one beat behind.

"People who'd never touched a game before played this one," Glitch said. "Grandparents. Whole families, all at once."

"That's kind of the whole point of games, though, right?" Theo said. "Everyone gets a turn."

The scene shifted again, this time to blocky green hills, cube-shaped trees, a blocky sun hanging low.

"Recognize this?" Glitch asked.

Theo laughed. "Obviously. That's Minecraft."

"**2011**," Glitch said. "A Swedish developer named **Markus Persson** — people called him 'Notch' — released it. It went on to become the **best-selling video game ever made**."

"People just... build stuff," Theo said. "No levels, no boss fight, just build whatever you want."

"Sound familiar?" Glitch asked, nodding toward Theo's half-finished stadium, still glowing somewhere back in his actual bedroom.

One more fold of the screen, and they stood in front of a tall glass building, a sign out front reading THE STRONG — WORLD VIDEO GAME HALL OF FAME.

"**2015**," Glitch said. "Rochester, New York. A whole museum, just for games. Everything you've seen tonight has a shelf in there somewhere."

Theo looked back down the long hallway of memories behind him — the oscilloscope, the jammed quarters, the buried cartridges, the plumber, the blue hedgehog — all the way back to one bouncing green dot on a tiny screen.

"That's a lot of people," he said, "all trying to fix the same ball problem."

"And you're about to go fix yours," Glitch said.

The screen folded shut like a closing laptop lid, and Theo was back on his bedroom floor, controller cold against his palm, a cursor blinking patiently in the corner of his screen.

He typed in a new gravity number. The ball dropped, bounced once, and rolled true.

Theo grinned at the blinking green cursor. "Thanks for the assist."

The cursor blinked twice, almost like a wink, and went still.

facts.text: In 1958, physicist William Higinbotham built 'Tennis for Two,' shown on an oscilloscope at Brookhaven National Laboratory.
In 1962, MIT student Steve Russell and friends programmed 'Spacewar!' on a PDP-1 computer.
Engineer Ralph Baer, later called 'the father of video games,' built a TV prototype, the 'Brown Box,' in the late 1960s.
Baer's prototype became the Magnavox Odyssey, the first home video game console, released in 1972.
Also in 1972, Nolan Bushnell and Ted Dabney founded Atari and released the arcade hit Pong.
A popular story says an early Pong arcade machine jammed from too many quarters, showing the game's fast popularity.
The Atari 2600, launched in 1977, let players swap in plastic cartridges instead of one built-in game.
In 1978, designer Tomohiro Nishikado created Space Invaders for Taito, sparking a worldwide arcade craze.
In 1980, designer Toru Iwatani created Pac-Man for Namco, said to be inspired by a pizza missing a slice.
The video game crash of 1983 shrank the North American market after stores were flooded with rushed, low-quality games.
A famous story says unsold Atari cartridges, including E.T., were buried in a New Mexico landfill, confirmed by diggers in 2014.
Nintendo revived the US market in 1985 with the NES, bundled with Super Mario Bros.
Shigeru Miyamoto designed Super Mario Bros. in 1985, starring plumber Mario, gaming's most famous character.
In 1984, Soviet scientist Alexey Pajitnov invented the puzzle game Tetris at a computer center in Moscow.
In 1991, Sega released Sonic the Hedgehog, a fast blue mascot created to compete with Nintendo's Mario.
Sony entered consoles in 1994 with the PlayStation, using CDs for fuller video and sound.
The 1993 shooter Doom popularized multiplayer matches and inspired early LAN parties linking computers together.
In 2006, Nintendo's Wii used motion controllers, drawing in players who had rarely gamed before.
Swedish developer Markus 'Notch' Persson released Minecraft in 2011; it later became the best-selling video game ever.
The World Video Game Hall of Fame opened in 2015 at The Strong museum in Rochester, New York.
